This research focuses on a wireless communication system that incorporates multiple access techniques and orthogonal spaces to enhance security, using an optimization approach to minimize a security risk metric. The optimization target, representing the probability of an unauthorized user decrypting information, is minimized while adhering to constraints on power usage, dimensionless security factors, and fr frontier conditions. To solve this problem, we apply numerical and intuitive methods to optimize power and space allocation at different nodes. Additionally, we verified the efficacy of our approach through simulations conducted on various systems.

Quantum emitters coupled with photonic topological systems can facilitate the creation of non-local entangled states between the emitters and protected edge modes. To achieve this, we propose using a diode-based unit cell to create a non-abrupt interface between two segments of a photonic topological material. This structure allows for the control of light flow and enables full synchronization between two isolated regions by coupling the emitters to the protected edge modes. As a result, we demonstrate that multiple emitters can be connected to a single source of light and that they entangle with the protected edge modes. Furthermore, this structure can be expanded to create a multiplexing system that can selectively create non-local entangled states between any two emitters.

In the complex and ever-changing urban environment, predicting other road users' actions and responding to traffic signals is crucial for the safe operation of automated vehicles. We analyze how the yellow and red phases of traffic signals influence the motion of cabin occupants and impact the trajectory planning of automated vehicles approaching urban intersections. By examining the effects of these phases on the motion of third-party vehicles and pedestrian groups, we demonstrate the importance of yellow and red phases in determining the best course of action for automated vehicles. Our research utilizes a motion prediction model that takes into account the past movements of all road users to estimate their future actions at a given intersection. This model is particularly valuable because it doesn't require high-speed communication with other vehicles, thus making it suitable for a vast majority of automated vehicles. As these vehicles approach an intersection, their trajectory planning is optimized with a focus on minimizing braking and the resulting discomfort for occupants, as well as avoiding costly and unnecessary acceleration. We provide data on the diversity of movements observed at two different urban intersections in the United States.

We introduce TextWorldExpress, a new fast parser generator for TextWorld, a challenging text-based game simulation. Created using Pyparsing, TextWorldExpress achieves significantly higher speeds and more efficient performance compared to previous parsing methods. Our tests demonstrate that TextWorldExpress runs 8-10 times faster than the standard Python implementation and 5-7 times faster than specialized parsers, while also reducing memory usage by half. Furthermore, TextWorldExpress exhibits superior performance in both simple and complex scenarios, paving the way for larger-scale text-based game simulations.

Deep learning algorithms have become the standard for achieving high accuracy in various tasks, primarily employing Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). As data size increases, cross-domain information needs to be integrated, leading to immense computational demands and substantial memory requirements. As a result, designing efficient hardware for deep learning applications has become a pressing issue. To address this challenge, a novel FDHT-LSTM hardware architecture is proposed, which enhances the performance of time-series prediction tasks. By combining a Fast Data-parallel HT (FDHT) storage system with a high-efficiency data processing unit, this architecture significantly improves throughput and energy efficiency. In comparison to traditional tensor decomposed model-oriented hardware, FDHT-LSTM exhibits superior performance, with a throughput increase of up to 3.5 times and energy efficiency enhancement of up to 2.2 times. Moreover, this architecture demonstrates flexibility in accommodating various deep learning architectures. To further optimize the FDHT-LSTM design, a through-put-driven Area-Time product (AT) co-design methodology is proposed, enabling efficient memory allocation and unit pipelining. As a result, FDHT-LSTM achieves a significant AT product improvement, leading to a 2.5 times increase in throughput with a 1.4 times area efficiency improvement. Ultimately, this work showcases a high-performance FDHT-LSTM hardware architecture and provides a comprehensive co-design methodology for designing efficient deep learning hardware systems.

We investigated various efficient methods for enhancing the efficiency of NLP through improved data, focusing on enhancing the performance of a fixed, high-quality dataset under varying batch sizes. Our findings were validated across four primary NLP applications, incorporating the BART model in three contexts and a BART-based sequence-to-sequence model in the remaining context. Ultimately, our research discovered that data augmentation can yield up to 8.5% greater improvements than the best baseline strategy, with the most substantial enhancement observed at smaller batch sizes. Additionally, our results revealed that sampling-based methods deliver the most consistent and substantial enhancements, surpassing the performance of the original model by an average of 4.3% across all batch sizes.

A working version of the Weak Gravity Conjecture (WGC) has been proposed by Heckman and Seidensticker, requiring a minimum self-binding energy for particles in anti-de Sitter space. We demonstrate that this self-binding energy criterion equates to a condition on the charge-to-mass ratio, thus making the WGC tantamount to the usual charge condition found in flat space. We further analyze the self-binding energy condition within a 4d $\mathcal{N}=2$ supergravity theory, revealing that it poses non-trivial constraints on the masses and charges of BPS states in anti-de Sitter space. We develop an invariant entropy function lattice framework to satisfactorily address these constraints, ultimately establishing that the self-binding energy condition yields the expected charge condition in a consistent AdS/CFT correspondence. We also examine the implications of this framework on the WGC in a 4d $\mathcal{N}=4$ supergravity theory with an arbitrary number of Abelian vectors.

To simulate multiple coexisting quantum states within a single material, we draw upon the model-space approach which draws inspiration from many-body physics theories. In this method, we parameterize a target Hamiltonian in terms of a set of simpler'model' Hamiltonians, and then perform a series of exact diagonalizations to capture the essential interactions. We've developed an efficient algorithm to automatically select the most crucial model spaces based on their relevance to the target ground state. Our method is particularly effective at identifying unusual, symmetry-breaking states which are often overlooked by conventional symmetry-based approaches. Using this model, we successfully isolated a pair of contrasting magnetic states within a 1T' CaV$_4$O$_6$ crystal using ab initio calculations. These states, which involve different spatial arrangements of V$^{2+}$ ions, were previously underestimated in terms of their symmetry and have been misinterpreted in experiments due to their highly delocalized nature. We highlight the potential of this model-space approach to accelerate the discovery of these exotic states and facilitate the development of associated zero-energy states, which are crucial for implementing topological quantum chemicals.

Given a local ring R with a specific idempotent element $\theta$, we examine the zero submodule of the $\theta$-torsion local cohomology module $H^i_{\frak p} (R)$, where $i = 1, 2$ and the maximal ideal $\frak p$ of $R$. This investigation aims to understand the connection between this submodule and the function $e_0 (R)$, which determines whether the local ring R is faithfully rational. With specific local rings R, we analyze the structure of the zero submodule and its relationship with $e_0 (R)$. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound for the zero submodule when R is faithfully rational. This study specifically utilizes the $\theta$-torsion local cohomology module $H^1_{\frak p} (R)$, and our findings complement the general approaches discussed in [ENNY].

A common issue in designing secondary electricity markets is the challenge of achieving exact solutions, which is crucial for the effectiveness of all-or-none order designs, such as in redispatch markets. All-or-none designs require bidders to accept the entire amount of a successful offer or reject it entirely. To overcome this challenge, researchers have proposed methods for approximating optimal solutions, but these methods have limitations, such as high computational demands or unreliable outcomes. In contrast, the paper by Kühn and van der Vlerk demonstrates that exact optimal solutions can be determined for a significant class of all-or-none order designs through straightforward mathematical calculations. The paper specifically examines redispatch markets and demonstrates that the optimal outcome can be calculated directly, without the need for sophisticated algorithms, by rearranging the market equilibrium equation into a simple linear formula. The paper also investigates the implications of an all-or-none design on the grid operator's procurement strategy, revealing that it can lead to the grid operator overpaying for certain services. The paper concludes by highlighting the practical applications of this finding, which can be utilized by market participants to anticipate the outcomes of all-or-none designs, or by regulators who wish to understand the effects of this design on the grid operator's procurement strategy, particularly in relation to the issue of overpayment.

In 2006, P. Bateman and A. Horn formulated a conjecture relating Galois groups to polynomial equations in a finite field. This work aims to extend their hypothesis to function fields over a finite field and showcase the predicted Galois group realizations for a specific family of polynomial equations in those fields. Our approach builds upon the work of K. Harvey, who demonstrated a connection between the Bateman-Horn conjecture and volumes of orbits in the Galois group. This research also demonstrates that the predicted Galois group realizations generally comprise a large proportion of possible Galois groups in those fields. Additionally, it is proven that almost every possible Galois group realization in those fields arises from a polynomial equation of a specific type over those fields.

To evaluate the reliability of theoretical predictions for Higgs boson production at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), this study examines various combinations of jet reconstruction algorithms and top quark identification methods within the context of top quark pair production. Utilizing the Pythia 8 event generator and Delphes 3 for detector simulations, this research assesses top quark pair production's impact on detecting Higgs boson signals, specifically for the $pp \to H \to \gamma\gamma$ process with 13 TeV proton collisions and an integrated luminosity of 3000 pb$^{-1}$. For events featuring top quark decays, various strategies are evaluated for enhancing signal efficiency and suppress background, ultimately resulting in efficient reconstruction of the Higgs boson peak for both on-shell and off-shell scenarios. Nonetheless, fulfilling the LHC's precision potential relies heavily on accurately modeling top quark pair production.

To explore the fundamental properties of the Higgs boson and extend the Standard Model with additional scalar fields, physicists employ precision tests at the Large Hadron Collider, particularly examining the production and decay of the Higgs particle in its dominant form. This production method, known as gluon fusion, accounts for nearly the entire production of Higgs particles and is characterized by a two-pronged decay pattern, with the emission of two photons. To ensure that any extension of the Standard Model is consistent with this observation, researchers employ unitarity constraints, perturbative unitarity conditions, and precision tests of the Standard Model, focusing on the production and decay of the Higgs particle. A study employs a profile likelihood method to measure the branching ratio of this decay, using data from 36/fb of proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, and finds a value that agrees with the Standard Model prediction within a margin of uncertainty. Additionally, the search for extended scalar sectors, specifically a bottom-quark doublet, is conducted based on data from 36/fb of proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV and previous measurements at 7 and 8 TeV, and the results are used to derive unitarity constraints that are compared with a supersymmetric extension of the Standard Model.

Observations from the Cassini space telescope between 2009 and 2010 revealed a persistent, stable polar vortex in the Saturnian stratosphere, specifically at the north pole. For the following eight years, a comparable vortex was not detected. However, during the 2017-2018 period, detailed observations from the Saturn by Cassini and the Hubble Space Telescope showed that the north polar vortex had a stable core with minimal wind speed, surrounding by stronger winds. Additionally, this vision was compared with one taken in 2017 from the Hubble Space Telescope, which displayed a similar vortex in the southern hemisphere for the first time. It was found that the two hemispheres' polar vessels had distinct characteristics, with the Saturnian polar vessel being an ongoing, stable feature that covered multiple seasons, as opposed to the summer-vortex phenomenon in Saturn. Moreover, this was supported by a comprehensive analysis using the Saturnian zonal mean wind and temperature data, which showed that the vortex's stability was due to its location within the stratospheric critical layer and its relationship with the wind and temperature patterns in the Saturnian system.

We demonstrate that for the periodic Schrödinger equation under certain monotic potentials, solutions with initial data of finite regularization and significant growth will experience blow-up, counteracting a long-held belief rooted in classical reasoning about boundary effects. Our findings are supported by two primary arguments. Firstly, we utilize the Strichartz estimate in combination with the properties of the Schrödinger propagator to establish bounds on the growth of solutions in a bounded domain. Secondly, we leverage the discrete nature of the spectrum in a bounded domain to devise a more direct proof of blow-up for certain initial conditions.

Notably, we demonstrate in Part 3 that the principles of characteristic-zero commutative algebra have equivalents in positive-characteristic commutative algebra, under the assumption that the characteristic is large enough to avoid certain technical issues related to zero divisors.

We have conducted a comprehensive examination of the electronic structure near the metal-insulator transition in highly correlated systems with three dimensions, utilizing the Hubbard model and high-order perturbation theory on a cubic lattice. Our analysis utilized the density of states and spectral weight at different energy levels to gain insights. Firstly, we verified that the sum of spectral weight across the entire energy spectrum remains consistent with expectations for both metallic and insulating states. Nevertheless, we discovered a marked disparity in spectral distribution between these states, coupled with a marked shift in electronic localization across the metal-insulator transition. Notably, we found evidence suggesting that the breakdown of'sum rules of spectral weight' occurs during the metal-insulator transition, driven by the divergence of f-sum rules within a particular energy range that is infinitesimally small. Furthermore, we established an explicit connection between this development and the onset of electronic localization,,t, along with the formation of a gap in the density of states, through the correlation between related quantities.

We have successfully developed two methods to calculate the ground state properties of quantum one-dimensional double dark-solitons. The first approach utilizes a variational theory based on the Hartree-Fock state, while the second utilizes a binary mixture ofonic Bose-Einstein condensates. We then compare the two approaches by examining the density profile, momentum distribution, and structure factor of the double dark-soliton. Our findings demonstrate that both theories converge to the same result, and that the variational Hartree-Fock theory provides a precise description of the quantum state in question. Furthermore, we have identified that the density profile of the double dark-soliton evolves in a specific manner, exhibiting oscillatory behavior accompanied by the emission of monatomic solitons. We also derive a conservation rule for the total momentum within the double dark-soliton system, revealing a scaling relationship for the momenta of the incoming and scattered components. Additionally, we have simulated the interaction between two double dark-solitons and observed the creation of multiple solitons, including a triple dark-soliton state, demonstrating that their dynamics are highly complex and multi-faceted.

A new interpretation of symmetric double vector bundles is provided, framing them as the object of a broader category - the category of symplectic double vector bundles. This perspective allows for an equivalent definition of symmetric double vector bundles in terms of closed, symplectic forms defining analytic mappings between a double vector bundle and a vector bundle. A key aspect explored in the paper is the relationship between this category and the category of k-fold vector bundles - it is demonstrated that the latter arises from the former, with k representing the characteristic of a double vector bundle. This work extends the relationship between Kirillov's measure and geometric measure on orbits in simple Lie algebras, establishing a similar measure-orbit connection for para-Hermitian matrices.

A recent algorithm, the Non-uniform Discrete Fourier Transform based Filter Bank (NUFFB) method, is examined as a potential solution to phase retrieval issues in x-ray scattering experiments. This involves evaluating the NUFFB method's capability to estimate energy spectra from x-ray scattering data with a particular focus on its application to free electron lasers. Various data sets with different energy ranges and detector resolutions were used in the study. The results show that the NUFFB method can accurately reconstruct energy spectra, especially when the energy spread is small. However, it was found that the algorithm's performance declines in scenarios with larger energy spreads or higher order diffractions, likely due to its assumption of the four-fold periodicity of scattering patterns. To overcome this limitation, a new approach based on the NUFFB method is proposed, which takes into account the actual detector resolution rather than relying on it as a parameter. The modified algorithm demonstrates enhanced ability to handle a wider energy range, a critical capability for achieving high-energy spectrum resolution with current and future free electron lasers.

We've proposed using classical disordered statistical mechanics models to analyze quantum error correcting codes under noise. Using this approach, we transform a problem of protecting quantum states into a problem of averaging over random classical configurations. This method is particularly effective for exploring the performance of 5th-order quantum self-correcting codes via Monte Carlo simulations of related classical models. Our analysis reveals that the stability of these classical models corresponds to the stability of the associated quantum codes and enables us to map classical phase transitions to quantum tipping transitions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that precise calculations of classical critical temperatures can yield valuable insights into the performance of quantum self-correcting codes.

Tellurene is an exceptionally conductive two-dimensional material with numerous applications, however, achieving a non-trivial gap in Tellurene quantum wells has been a challenge. By utilizing a combination of strain engineering and superlattice layers, we successfully reduced the 2 MeV bulk band overlap in Tellurene to nearly zero. A notable non-trivial gap of approximately 10.5 MeV was created at the Gamma point, this gap can be adjusted through strain levels ranging from -2 to 2, also, it was observed that the gap increases with the average electron density in a way that is directly proportional. This breakthrough enables the possibility of creating superlattice layers that can manipulate both the gap and electron density in Tellurene quantum wells.

To account for blocking fractures, we modify the standard Darcy flow model while drawing on the Dirac-β function's approach. We introduce a family of simplified models that maintain mass balance within subdomains of blocking fractures, drawing on the double layer potential equation's solution for their parameterization. We then establish local existence and uniqueness of a weak solution for the modified model, leveraging the potential theory. Blocking fractures are modeled as planes intersecting the computational domain's boundary at a right angle. We demonstrate that our approach's approximations converge to the original PDE as the model's parameter approaches zero. This involves defining a family of nested nonoverlapping subdomains whose boundaries converge to the fractures' geometry. We prove that our approach's approximations conserve mass within the subdomains of blocking fractures and that they can handle complex, multiply blocked domain geometries. We also show that our approach's approximations' solutions' regularity is enhanced when compared to the standard Darcy flow model. We provide numerical results demonstrating the method's effectiveness.

We investigate the spin-valve behavior of ferromagnetic double layers made from two identical layers of a ferromagnetic semiconductor, using a finite difference method to solve the spin-resolved Boltzmann equation. Our calculations show that spin-valve resistance changes can be significantly controlled using a mild exchange field, particularly in the low-temperature and moderately low-exchange-field regime. At higher exchange fields, the spin-valve resistance change becomes nearly exchange-free, mainly influenced by the symmetry of the (001)-oriented semiconductors considered. The findings can help enable efficient spin-valve resistance change measurements in far-infrared spectroscopy.

The H0 validity tester introduces a comprehensive framework that encompasses diverse methods for evaluating statistical hypotheses. This framework's core component is a decision function, which generates a score for each hypothesis based on utility principles and p-value thresholds. The framework's strength lies in its ability to incorporate any decision function, either existing or custom-made, thus facilitating hypothesis evaluation. Furthermore, the framework provides a criterion for comparing the performance of different hypotheses, ultimately facilitating the selection of the best hypothesis through optimization. This approach can be executed using nested Monte Carlo evaluation, an efficient method for assessing the expected loss under a given utility function. The framework's utility-based approach is particularly valuable in complex settings where hypotheses cannot be directly compared. To demonstrate its effectiveness, the H0 validity tester is applied to a simplified version of the cluster identification problem and to real-life genetic data.

We release a large-scale corpus called DiscSense, which is comprised of writings by native French speakers, mapped with a wide range of discourse indicators and connection labels. Unlike other annotated corpora, which focus exclusively on connection labels or indicators of discourse, DiscSense covers both categories extensively. Our annotation tools and guidelines were particularly designed to distinguish between indicators of discourse that convey a connection's nature and those that don't. Additionally, they differentiate between paratactic and hypotactic relations. We differentiate between two types of relation labels: one that identifies the connection and a more detailed label that specifies the connection's kind. Our empirical studies show that models developed for low-to-medium density texts can effectively extract indicators of discourse and connection labels from DiscSense. However, these models' performance significantly declines when processing high-density texts. Building on BERT, a model that is fine-tuned on DiscSense yields a notable improvement in both indicators of discourse and connection labels, even in high-density texts. The code along with the annotated corpus and results are available for reproduction at this address: https://github.com/Alain-Gabriel-Courard-Hubert/DiscSense.

For years, researchers have been attempting to grasp the Mott-Seitz model's impact on the behavior of small clusters of alkali halides and hydrogen, particularly in relation to nonradiative decay. These efforts have been complicated by the absence of a clear measure of the energy needed to break chemical bonds in these small groups of atoms. In this study, researchers used a combination of theoretical chemistry and optical spectroscopy to determine this value for a cluster of four sodium atoms bonded to four oxygen atoms, which make up the dimer of a certain complex, for the first time. By comparing their findings with predictions made by the Mott-Seitz model, they were able to verify its accuracy and also learn more about the distribution of energies within these clusters. Additionally, this new understanding enabled them to accurately describe a type of optical transition that has been difficult to model reliably in the past. This breakthrough could make it possible to use the Mott-Seitz model to develop cluster series with specific properties in the future.

We introduce an innovative neural network training technique called forward propagation of errors, a method that diverges from standard backpropagation methods. During training, error gradients are calculated along the neural network's forward pass, allowing for faster and more energy-efficient computations. Our model utilizes synthetic data and compares the training outcomes of backpropagation and forward error propagation. The results show that both methods converge to similar neural network performances, and forward error propagation demonstrates a clear advantage in terms of computational speed and energy efficiency.

We investigate a $2$-dimensional model where matter fields take values in a general, non-trivial homotopy class and are minimally coupled to an external, uniform magnetic field. Using continuous monopole currents, our analysis establishes the existence of multiple skyrmion types based on the homotopy group of the target space. For a given, non-trivial homotopy class, all skyrmion configurations can be expressed as a linear combination of a limited set of fundamental solutions, collecting these fundamental solutions together forms a complete basis for the corresponding skyrmion states. We identify and classify distinct skyrmion types by their linear combination structure in various spacetime backgrounds, including those represented by constant Euclidean metrics, cylindrical spaces, and toroidal environments. Furthermore, we examine the interplay between magnetic field and potential nonlinear target space configurations through field redefinition up to a non-trivial identity, drawing parallels with the construction of skyrmions in the $CP^2$ model.

It have been mathematically proven that in the Hartree-Fock approach, for weak to moderate electron-electron Coulomb interactions, the difference between total energies from iterations of the Hartree-Fock method, as they converge to a self-consistent equilibrium, follows a simple and specific pattern which can be approximated by a quadratic relationship. This finding can be explained in a straightforward manner within the framework of a harmonic oscillator model. Additionally, the speed of convergence is directly influenced by the strength of the electron-electron interactions, with stronger interactions leading to slower convergence. This result has significant implications, as it means that in cases of large systems where the Hartree-Fock method is employed, significant computational effort might be required to achieve a high degree of precision.

In complex networks, the interaction between dynamic and structural disorder in map tasks leads to a highly unpredictable environment, prompting a reevaluation of previous theories on synchronization transitions. Using a novel multi-dimensional parameter scan method on large-scale randomly assembled network architectures, this study reveals a sudden and drastic increase in explosive synchronization among a subset of highly connected "hub" nodes. Further analysis indicates that the emergence of rapid synchronization near the critical point is attributed to a specific robustness of the network, derived from its ability to filter out erratic dynamics during the time scaling of oscillations. Consequently, this filtered state of affairs amplifies the effect of small-scale structural changes on the network, ultimately propelling the system towards explosive synchronization.

We examine a matrix optimization problem where the objective function can be factored into two sets of variables, $x$ and $y$, with the constraint that $x$ and $y$ must follow the pattern of certain given matrices $\mathcal{K}$ and $\mathcal{H}$. By defining a convex function $f(x,y)$ that is strongly convex and smooth, we can determine a specific regime where the geodesic distance between two optimal solutions $(x_1,y_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2)$ is equivalent to the Euclidean distance between $(x_1,y_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2)$. To achieve this, we must establish that the optimal solutions $(x_1,y_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2)$ belong to the prescribed matrix patterns $\mathcal{K}$ and $\mathcal{H}$. By doing so, we can significantly speed up the convergence rate of various algorithms, including Nesterov's, to an almost linear time complexity of $\mathcal{O}(1/t^2)$ for our specific matrix optimization problem.

In 1990, Yang and Yang proposed a conjecture that, in bipartite graphs with a maximum degree of 3, every edge can be colored using a maximum of 2k, where k represents the smallest number greater than the logarithm base 2 of the number of edges, provided it is an integer. This conjecture was confirmed for certain types of graphs but not the general case. Now, we have established that a specific class of triangle-free bipartite graphs can achieve a 2k-edge coloring with an integer k greater than the logarithm base 2 of the number of edges.

The purpose of this paper is to provide identities that connect Gauss sums to Dirichlet L-functions, extending earlier findings. Specifically, we establish identities for $\Lambda(s)^2$, $\Lambda(s)\Lambda(2-s)$, and $\Lambda(s)\Lambda(3-s)$, where $\Lambda(s)$ represents Dirichlet L-functions. These identities facilitate a deeper understanding of the observed connections between Gauss sums and Dirichlet L-functions in recent studies.

Researchers anticipate discovering gravitational wave backgrounds generated by heavy particles interacting with each other in the early universe. These expectations might be misled if these heavy particles prompt the creation of long-lived, particle-like objects that, when interacting with each other or with standard particles, produce gravitational waves of varying frequencies. Such a scenario could prevent current experiments from identifying a gravitational wave background even if the standard model particles that produce the background have an extremely low probability of occurrence. It is demonstrated in this paper that even when the probability of standard model particles generating a background is as low as 10^-10, a significant number of backgrounds can still be produced, which could potentially conflict with present and future experiments' ability to detect these backgrounds, especially in the lowscale LISA mission. Additionally, it is found that even a small probability of standard model particles producing backgrounds could significantly reduce the parameter space that best explains cosmic microwave background anomalies. Furthermore, it is found that even a small probability of standard model particles generating backgrounds can significantly reduce the parameter space that best explains cosmic microwave background anomalies.

We've been analyzing the movement of helical microswimmers that interact with a diverse range of particle interactions, including those influenced by the snowman effect, where the helix's tip generates opposite forces compared to its base. By combining these effects with the interactions of Brownian motion and surface tension, we determine the impact on a swimmer's locomotion. Additionally, we explore the possibility of optimizing swimmers with varying helical shapes, including those with symmetrical and asymmetrical designs, incorporating the effects of snowman-like movement, surface tension, and dimensionless particle interaction. Our analysis demonstrates that highly efficient swimmers can be developed, achieving up to 26 times faster locomotion compared to previously thought optimal designs.

This study explores the Hamming distance from Nash Equilibrium (NE) in both individual and social learning scenarios within the Wright-Fisher process for the electroencephalography dataset previously analyzed in [1]. To accomplish this, we run the Wright-Fisher process multiple times to determine the average Hamming distance from NE, even when considering the most basic learning case, namely the Wright-Fisher process with the learning rate set to 1.0. Our results reveal a clearer neccessity for a large population size in order to achieve a Hamming distance from NE of less than 10 for both social and individual learning. Furthermore, our data shows a greater Hamming distance from NE for social than individual learning. This phenomenon was anticipated, as the variation in social learning is more significant than in individual learning, with an observed Hamming distance from NE of around 30 for social learning and 10 for individual learning, even when the population size is set to 1000. Another key finding of our analysis is the presence of two distinct phases in the Wright-Fisher process: a more rapid phase with a larger variation in population fitness, and a slower phase with a more stable fitness close to the NE. This variation in the Wright-Fisher process is captured through a 2-tier exponential distribution, with the distinction between these two phases occurring at the time T*=log(2)/λ.

The rapid evolution of online threats necessitates enhanced malware detection along with richer security knowledge. To achieve this, we develop innovative techniques for both malicious code and textual data analysis. Firstly, by introducing a novel bidirectional LSTM algorithm, we significantly improve the accuracy of security concept extraction from textual content. Secondly, we develop a pioneering approach using bidirectional LSTMs and attention mechanisms to enhance the effectiveness of malware feature extraction from binary code. Utilizing a custom-designed dataset, our methods demonstrate a notable increase in performance when compared to conventional approaches.

We introduce a new mixed opinion formation model that combines elements from the Mersenne map and the North, Shirley, and Mehta models. This hybrid model incorporates both binary opinion states and continuous magnetization levels. Our analysis focuses on a large number of agents and their corresponding system behavior. Equivalently, this can be studied through a dual description using the Mersenne map and Ising model. We derive exact expressions for the stationary magnetization and temperature in the Mersenne-Ising system. Additionally, we investigate temperature equilibrium between separate Ising ensembles and the Mersenne map. Our results show that the average magnetization in the mixed model matches that of a corresponding pure Ising model, with appropriate scaling. Furthermore, temperature equilibrium is achieved when the Mersenne map's parameter reaches a specific, previously unknown value, previously only defined for non-equilibrium conditions.

We demonstrate a mathematical model to analyze the dispersion of COVID-19 through respiratory droplets, developing a relationship between the distance they travel and the size of the droplets. We investigate the impact of varying weather conditions, air humidity, temperature, and droplet size on transmission, utilizing numerical simulations. The model is applied to examine infection dynamics within closed spaces, considering factors like room size, ventilation, and the activity level of individuals. We use available data to estimate the effectiveness of face masks in reducing droplet spread, finding that they significantly slow infection spread, especially in windy conditions, and we investigate the benefits of improving ventilation by increasing air exchange rate in closed environments.

The convergence of deep learning methods with vast data sets and subtle
errors to achieve precision in solving complex inverse problems is a striking
phenomenon. This idea can be distilled into a mathematical framework that
transforms a difficult inverse problem into an efficiently solvable issue.
We demonstrate how this approach unlocks significant advancements in areas
such as image denoising, deblurring, and reconstruction from incomplete
information, and undersampled measurements, outperforming traditional methods
with vast data sets.

This study examines a specific equality between ordinary and symbolic powers of edge ideals within a particular type of graph, oriented and weighted, utilizing a specific parameter $\chi$. We initially establish that equality holds for a broad range of graphs, oriented and weighted, including those with linearly independent support and those with interconnected components. Furthermore, we define a new invariant $\chi$ based on the number of distinct components in a weighted oriented graph, demonstrating that equality holds if and only if $\chi$ meets a certain minimum threshold. Additionally, we explore how $\chi$ evolves with changes to the graph, oriented and weighted, and provide a lower bound for its values in various scenarios, ultimately concluding that equalities between powers of edge ideals and their symbolic powers have fundamental connections to the topological properties of weighted oriented graphs.

Using the holographic principle, we calculate the partition functions for SU(N) and U(N) in various dimensions. Our calculations show that the partition functions for these groups have distinct differences as N approaches a finite value, particularly in 3-dimensional space where the dual gravity shares features with the Poincare patch. In 4-dimensional space, we find the partition functions for SU(N) and U(N) to have similar differences as the 3-dimensional case. Additionally, we determine the free energy for SU(N) and U(N) in 5-dimensional space and a Kaluza-Klein compactification of the torus, and demonstrate that the Casimir energy for these groups can be derived from the free energy.

Deep neural networks deployed in sensitive applications require confident security and reliability, which involves preventing sensitive data from being accessed improperly. Even with high-performance hardware, implementing suitable limitations on data access pattern restrictions can prevent silent data corruptions in real-time applications. Non-uniform hardware configurations, such as diverse memory banks with varying access speeds, offer opportunities to enforce data access restrictions through hardware means. Based on a simple, general hardware model, we demonstrate the effectiveness of non-uniform data access restriction methods in preventing silent data corruptions, which can significantly enhance the reliable deployment of deep neural networks, such as convolutional neural networks, by reducing the necessary memory capacity by at least 20% on average. We further show that optimizing memory bank sizes according to the data access patterns of specific hardware configurations can achieve an additional 10% in memory reduction. Our approach to enforcing data access restrictions involves modifying the neural network training process, which yields high accuracy and can be achieved with minimal computational overhead. We also provide a general framework for optimizing memory configurations in relation to hardware costs.

We've developed multiple novel graph algorithms to solve complex problems arising from netting mechanisms, a crucial process in the financial industry. By leveraging these algorithms, institutions can optimize their interbank claims and settlements, ultimately contributing to enhanced financial stability. Our research focuses on a scenario where multiple parties engage in reciprocal claims and settlements, which can be interpreted as a bipartite graph capturing the netting relationships. To find an optimal solution, we've devised two general approaches for two specific types of netting mechanisms: an exhaustive method and a local optimization approach. We've also employed two particular algorithms within the local optimization approach: the Metropolis-Hastings and the Monte-Carlo simulations. Through comparative analysis using realistic data scenarios, we've demonstrated the efficiency and effectiveness of our algorithms. Furthermore, we've explored the application of these algorithms to a more general case of multi-level netting, and have obtained valuable insights that could direct future research towards better solving this complex problem.

We explore the implications of a generalized Jordanian twist that maintains a specific ordering, establishing its equivalence to a simple Jordanian twist. This investigation arises from analyzing the deformation of Yangian constructions in 1+1 dimensional integrable systems, specifically for the SU(N) algebra.

We introduce a cutting-edge approach called residual connection-based multi-task learning, which significantly boosts performance in low-resource language name tagging. Utilizing a publicly available corpus of annotated names in high-resource languages and a available corpus in low-resource languages, we develop a joint model that leverages the learned representations from both sources. By incorporating a residual connection-based encoder, a simple but effective decoder, and a type-based character attention mechanism, we achieve a notable improvement. Our method demonstrates a substantial advantage over current state-of-the-art techniques in low-resource language name tagging, with only 1000 labeled examples. Notably, we demonstrate a notable improvement of 11.4% over the baseline model and outperform it by 4.3% on average across eight diverse languages.

Our research offers a comprehensive overview of particle ratios from $p$+Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV, including protons colliding with lithium, carbon, aluminum, and oxygen targets at 3.5 TeV, and lead colliding with oxygen at 2 TeV, collected by the ALICE experiment at the LHC. These findings demonstrate trends in particle production that emulate those seen in proton-proton collisions, with variations that depend on the collision system's size and temperature. For instance, the ratio of pions to protons exhibits an increase with rising centrality in $p$+Pb and Xe+Xe collisions, while the ratio of kaons to protons displays a decline with increasing centrality in $p$+Pb, Xe+Xe, and Pb+Pb collisions. Furthermore, the calculated $K^+/p$ and $\pi./p$ ratios, after accounting for temperature and centrality, reveal distinct patterns that correlate with the collision system's size. These observations support existing models of particle production on a partonic level, with implications for our understanding of hadronization in heavy ion and proton-nucleus collisions.

The increasing size of dialog state tracking (DST) datasets comes with the inconvenience of incorporating numerous noisy labels. These untrusted data points can cause significant issues during the training process, leading to suboptimal performance. We propose a method to eliminate noisy labels from the dataset, drawing inspiration from the neighborhood low-density mechanism used in neighbor selection. By incorporating the hardness of neighbor examples into the training process, our approach achieves the best results. We utilize the BERT encoder to represent dialogue state descriptions and the transition-based transition system for transition dynamics. Our method evaluates the effectiveness of removing noisy labels on the all-encompassing DSTC7 benchmark, yielding outstanding results with the best mean F1 score of 73.01, surpassing the current state-of-the-art by a significant margin of 3.5%. Additionally, our method demonstrates notable robustness in response to the corruption of clean data with an increasing amount of noisy labels.

Inspired by the potential impact of changing urban infrastructure on social dynamics, we develop a theoretical framework and use the example of a Victorian-era London water network to illustrate its applications. This analytical method assigns a degree of 'contagion risk' to each network node based on its connectivity and flow patterns. By correlating historical water network data with corresponding maps of riot activity, we aim to demonstrate a plausible connection between the topology of the water network and the riot spreads. Furthermore, we show that this approach is versatile and can be adapted to explore relationships between other types of urban infrastructure and societal dynamics, such as electricity grids and news dissemination, or sewer systems and disease transmission.

Our investigation aims to evaluate the precision of star formation rate (SFR) estimates produced by the Prospector framework, specifically focusing on its use of g, r, i, z, J, H, Ks photometry and B band luminosity to predict SFRs and masses for 303,000 galaxies from the KPyCES sample. By comparing the observed and inferred values of these quantities, as well as the scatter at each metallicity, we found that adding B band luminosity significantly improves the accuracy of SFR estimates. Additionally, we found that a wide range of chemical abundances can maintain a consistent 0.12 dex scatter in mass estimates and a 0.34 dex scatter in SFR estimates. Furthermore, we found that adding B band luminosity significantly improves the accuracy of SFR estimates and examined the implications of using this method in the BASS survey.

We provide an investigation into the maximum possible number of polynomials that can be expressed as a sum of squares over the Gram spectrahedron defined by a given set of symmetric matrices, assuming a specific positive definiteness condition. This research is applicable to various applications such as control theory, system design, and optimization, which are often formulated using matrix and polynomial variables. For example, designing a controllable continuous-time LTI system via a matrix transfer matrix, or a controllable discrete-time LTI system via its transfer matrix, can be both represented within the Gram spectrahedron. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to the case of block diagonal matrices under a specific factorization, which is crucial for these applications. However, our approach is limited to forms of quadratic and cubic polynomials, which are fundamental building blocks for more complex polynomials. Finally, we outline potential future directions for stack-based or composition-based polynomials.

To investigate neutrino interactions with a highly sensitive probe, the FASERν experiment at CERN's HL-LHC will provide valuable insights into both neutrino and anti-neutrino scattering, with a focus on lepton non-unitarity and certain rare proton decay processes. By analyzing final state particles produced in the decay volume, located behind the IRD (Intersecting Storage Rings) and far from the expected neutrino beams, the experiment can constrain neutrino properties. With an expected annual neutrino flux of around 8 x 10^10 ν/Proton/luminosity, the experiment can make significant contributions to both lepton non-unitarity and certain rare proton decay phenomena. In addition, by analyzing neutral current events with multi-particle final states, the experiment can place bounds on its own systematic uncertainties, which can be applied to other searches for rare neutrino processes.

Brzozowski's operator for regular expressions has been combined with set difference to create a symbolic decision procedure to determine if one regular expression is contained within another. This method forms the basis for our investigation into the properties and limitations of this procedure when applied to regular expressions over an infinite alphabet. We initially establish that, despite being decision-effective for containing regular expressions, this procedure is not Turing-complete when using an infinite alphabet. This finding is then supported by two separate proofs. Firstly, we demonstrate that Brzozowski's operator, along with set difference and containment, is sufficient for developing a context-free language recognizer. Secondly, a more direct proof is provided, based on the characteristics of infinite alphabets. We also provide a more efficient algorithm for evaluating contained-to-checking expressions, leading to a potential improvement in the performance of regular expression engines. This is achieved through the elimination of redundant computations during the intersection calculation. The new algorithm is then validated through benchmark tests, highlighting its superiority over existing methods.

Deep learning-based Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) algorithms have flourished in recent years due to their ability to combine visual and inertial data for accurate state estimation. Despite such success, a comprehensive comparison of these deep learning-based VIO systems in various scenarios has yet to be presented. In this work, we conduct an in-depth survey and comparison of prominent deep learning-based VIO approaches. We classify these algorithms into two categories based on their data processing methods and perform extensive experiments with publicly available datasets to evaluate and contrast their performance. Our findings are supplemented by an open-source implementation of our comparison, which includes implementation details and corresponding code.

We've developed a novel theory that connects higher-order Weyl semimetals to the idea of square-root topology in 3D systems. Our framework effectively describes the exotic transport properties of these complex materials using a simple formula derived from the Berry curvature and surface velocity near the Weyl points. By applying this formula, we're able to quantitatively analyze the anomalous Hall conductivity, magnetic properties, and topological protection in Weyl semimetals. Furthermore, we've demonstrated that the square-root topology is a fundamental concept by showing it directly relates to the non-Abelian monopole nature of Weyl points.

This study examines the effectiveness of edge finite elements in solving a data completion problem, where incomplete data is used to recover a full data set, specifically a function defined on a domain in RN. We investigate various approaches to achieving this goal, formulating the problem as an ill-posed minimization issue of a least squares type. Our primary concern is the impact of choosing edge finite elements, given that standard approaches can yield poor results, even if the elements are well-defined for functions in H^1(D). To address this, we focus on elements that provide equivalent approximation capabilities, allowing us to leverage their distinct advantages, such as better convergence with higher order elements or improved performance on non-smooth domains, all while ensuring numerical stability. We establish a priori error estimates for several element types, demonstrating that edge finite elements can yield optimal convergence rates, and validate our results with numerical experiments featuring various element types, domain types, and data configurations.

This paper delves into the properties of a specific vertex operator algebra, created from the affine superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$, for its simplest representation. We identify a set of associated generators and determine their expansion characteristics using intertwinning operators, essentially expressing the vertex operator algebra in terms of irreducible representations of $osp(1|2n)$. Furthermore, we derive the characteristic coefficients of these expansions, leading to a detailed understanding of the vertex operator algebra generated from the affine superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$, for its simplest representation.

In the context of knowledge amalgamation, a new training method for a student model is introduced that leverages a saliency-based approach. This method identifies specific components of the teacher model's knowledge that are most relevant to improving the student's performance. Unlike conventional training methods that aim to compress the entire teacher model, this approach can achieve comparable performance with significantly fewer parameters. Experiments conducted on various datasets and applications, such as image classification, natural language inference, and speech recognition, demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, with the ability to accurately identify salient components and significantly reduce the parameters required for the student model.

Previous research suggested that grid cells contribute to the brain's efficient mapping and navigation abilities, likely leveraging a stable self-localization system to facilitate exploration. However, our findings indicate that external environmental cues play a significant role in maintaining grid cell functionality and generating periodic mapping patterns. In an experimental setting, we observed that grid cells in freely moving rats only manifest periodic mapping features, including activity patterns and island sizes, when the rats are navigating in environments with consistent visual and tactile features. When we altered key environmental cues, such as removing a prominent wall or changing floor textures, grid cells immediately adjusted their mapping patterns to reflect these changes. These adjustments occur even when the changes are minimal, underscoring the crucial role of sensory perceptions in shaping grid cell functionality and the self-localization system. Ultimately, our findings suggest that grid cells serve as a sensory-driven filter, refining environmental information to generate a simplified and efficient representation of the surrounding space.

The development of a star's magnetic cycle is influenced by two opposing processes: kinematic dynamos, which are driven by turbulent flows and operate outside of thermal equilibrium, and pseudo-dynamic processes, which maintain equilibrium through heat flux and heat generation. The former tends to prevail in rapidly rotating stars, the latter in slowly rotating stars. The rotation of a star can be tied to its magnetic cycle strength through the angular momentum conservation, which relates magnetic cycle energy to rotation rate energy. The presentation of this concept is visually demonstrated through a diagram of energy ratios. The relationship between magnetic cycle energy and rotation rate energy is further discussed for kinematic dynamos and pseudo-dynamic processes. The case of kinematic dynamos is mathematically modeled using the Stewartson layer equation. The conservation of angular momentum leads to an increase in the strength of magnetic cycle energy as the rotation rate of a star decreases, resulting in the possibility of spinstability. The condition for spinstability is derived from the model. The spinstability of kinematic dynamos is confirmed through numerical simulations of the Stewartson layer equation. The spinstability of pseudo-dynamic processes is demonstrated through numerical simulations of the Wulfman equation. The conservation of angular momentum must consider the conservation of specific angular momentum, leading to the possibility of spinstability in kinematic dynamos, but not pseudo-dynamic processes, which are influenced by the flow's overall angular momentum conservation, not specific angular momentum conservation. The spinstability of kin

We establish an initial count of four distinct S4 quartic fields that extend the rational numbers, ensuring a specific condition is met - that a particular family of elliptic curves, defined over these fields, maintain a rational rank of zero. Additionally, we outline criteria for identifying more such fields, suggesting the possibility of an infinite number of instances within the family of S4 quartic extensions. This achievement is complemented by a analysis, demonstrating that for fields which extend the rational numbers by means of a degree two extension, conditions similar to those initially set, are not sufficiently met, thus establishing that no corresponding gain in rank, as defined by the Langlands program, occurs for a family of elliptic curves in these situations.

We investigate the time-dependent production of entropy irreversibility following a quench in a quantum system, which can be applied to both equilibrated and isolated systems. Our approach utilizes a heat map to analyze the full time profile of entropy generation, including both initial and asymptotic components, and demonstrates that the total entropy produced during a quench at any given time is finite in systems with a discrete spectrum. Additionally, we derive a straightforward formula for calculating the total entropy produced in a finite system over an infinite duration, which is directly proportional to the system's temperature raised to a power depending on the interaction and spectrum density. This new understanding reveals that critical behaviors in entropy production are induced by critical behaviors in the two-point correlation function. Our findings are further illustrated using a quantum Ising chain with a uniform magnetic field, where different quench protocols are explored to showcase distinct time profiles of entropy generation. This research builds on our previous work, extending the application of the Heisenberg picture to both equilibrated and isolated systems, and providing novel insights into the entanglement dynamics of systems with a discrete spectrum.

We investigate the time-evolution of a system interacting with an environment, focusing on the time-twirling of the combined system-state and its relation to distinguishability time in non-unitary dynamics. It is demonstrated that twirling-time evolution is governed by a integral representation similar to the one for distinguishability time, enabling the identification of the most fiducial state in a given state ensemble. Additionally, it is shown that the twirling-time spectrum is contained in the spectrum of the Hamiltonian and that spectral singularities control the rate of approach to the time-twilled state, with possible delays induced by a non-Fredholm Hamiltonian. Cases such as system and environment forming a composite system, system interacting with an environment through a reservoir, and system coupled to an infinite environment are specifically analyzed.

We establish that a nondegenerate regular simplex within the unit cube $Q_n$ exists only when the number of interpolation nodes $k$ falls within the range $n \leq k \leq n^2$. Additionally, we demonstrate that the set $S_{\Delta^k}$ of all nondegenerate regular simplices of size $k$ is extensive over the unit cube $Q_n$, for any $n \geq 2$ when $k \geq n^2$.

We examined the carrier concentrations in etched silicon substrates and buffer oxide etched silicon substrates.  The carrier concentration in etched silicon was found to be no more than 1 x 10^16 per/cm^3, while in buffer oxide etched silicon it ranged from 1 x 10^16 to 3 x 10^16 per/cm^3.  A correlation existed between these concentrations and the oxide thickness in the etched silicon, but not in the buffer oxide etched silicon.  The faster etch rate for the (100) orientation over the (111) orientation, which we initially observed, was found to be influenced by the presence of the oxide layer, with the (100) orientation etching at a faster rate only when the oxide layer was absent.  A note is also made about the presence of metallic contamination in the etched materials.

This paper contributes to the long-term goal of relating twisted homotopy K-theory to algebraic K-theory through cdh descent and Milnor excision, confirming these developments for global fields and showing that they lead to a description of twisted homotopy K-theory in terms of algebraic K-theory.

The evolution of an exoplanet's atmosphere may be shaped by a continuous cycle between its interior and exterior layers. This cycle involves the generation of atmospheric waves that form and develop as they travel through the planet, eventually breaking down into turbulent motions and generating atmospheric circulation patterns. In turn, these circulation patterns give rise to conditions favorable for habitability, such as atmospheric retention and stellar insolation, that in turn influence the planet's evolution within its interior. This process contributes to the synthesis of volatile species in the atmosphere and influences core-mantle insulation, ultimately affecting heat transfer and, in turn, the planet's evolutionary track. Using a simplified 3D model, we simulate a range of scenarios to study the effects of this cycling on planetary evolution. Our results indicate that this cycling can have a significant impact on planetary evolution, potentially mitigating the loss of atmospheric volatiles and influencing core-mantle heat transfer. However, the exact effects also depend on various factors, including the heat transfer efficiency within the mantle and the core and the rates of volatile species synthesis and retention.

In this work, we employed high-speed computational methods and molecular dynamics simulations to examine 1,2-propanediol (1,2-PDO) and 1,3-propanediol (1,3-PDO) as models of small ring alcohols. Specifically, we investigated how these systems interact with water and anhydrous environments, and how they produce methyl cations. Our results show that 1,2-PDO forms an intramolecular hydrogen bond, which hinders the production of methyl cations when compared to 1,3-PDO. However, 1,2-PDO still yields a higher rate of methyl cation production than expected, indicating a degree of proton transfer between oxygen atoms. This effect is more pronounced in anhydrous conditions. Our data also reveal that water enhances the methyl cation production from 1,2-PDO by breaking the hydrogen bond, and that 1,2-PDO exhibits two distinct types of ring structures in anhydrous conditions, which contribute differently to methyl cation formation. These findings provide a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying methyl cation production from PDO in various environments.

In quantum computing, tensor networks and parametrized quantum circuits (PQCs) are distinct tools for achieving computational goals. Tensor networks, originating from the study of many-body systems in condensed matter physics, serve as a versatile framework that encompasses various circuits, including those for quantum simulation. Our research reveals that incorporating unitary transformations within these networks' local descriptors significantly enhances their expressive capability, effectively reducing the equivalent circuit size while maintaining or improving the accuracy of computations. Specifically, this strategy shows substantial size reductions in models of two distinct applications: the multipartite entanglement transition and the Bell-state amplitudes within the multiparticle Heisenberg model. As a result, this approach facilitates speedier execution and, with suitable unitary transformations, allows demonstration of complex phenomena that otherwise require unfeasibly long circuits. Furthermore, this strategy introduces a practical optimization approach for efficiently deriving highly accurate short PQCs within these tensor networks.

Cancer research has seen a shift in focus from traditional method analysis, such as Genomics and Signaling Pathway, towards visualizing and studying tissue samples. Abnormal cell growth within these tissues can provide valuable diagnostic information. A recent approach utilizes Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to distinguish between benign and malignant tissues, based on the spatial organization of cells within these tissues, by building on their morphological features. However, training a GNN on a new task requires a substantial amount of labeled data, which can be expensive and time-consuming to obtain. In response, we are proposing the use of a contrastive learning approach, called DeepMask, which uses a semi-supervised model to learn from both labeled and unlabeled tissue samples. This is achieved by defining a learning objective that minimizes the difference between masked tissue samples, resulting in multiple positive samples and a single negative sample for each encoded tissue representation. As a result, we are demonstrating the capability of DeepMask to classify tissue samples with significantly fewer required labels, at a rate of $4.76\pm0.75$x for the reduction of an average error of $13.53\pm2.35$%. Furthermore, we are showing that DeepMask outperforms existing state-of-the-art GNNs in cancer cell classification, based on the MITech dataset, with an overall accuracy of $85.19\pm3.35$%.

This paper introduces an explicit formula for the nonlinear Hawkes process's offspraw, which extends the general cluster Hawkes process, and details a nonparametric estimation method for the complex interaction network. The Hawkes process effectively captures interactions within multivariate point processes, but the implementation of the new method requires high computational power due to the intense optimization process of the network's parameters. We use simulated data to evaluate the accuracy of the method and demonstrate its application to a real-world dataset of Twitter posts.

We have developed a comprehensive software suite to create highly efficient, direct-nature simulations of the many-body problem present in astrophysical systems. At the heart of these simulations lies the Gforest library, which utilizes advanced computational techniques such as the Fast Multipole Method (FMM) to calculate gravitational interactions and accelerate their implementation on various high-performance computing platforms. Through a landmark MAO-8T supercomputer simulation, featuring over 8 billion time steps and incorporating a novel timing tool called TTT, we have extensively tested the performance and reliability of this software. At optimal tolerance levels, the simulations produce results that closely align with existing benchmarks, and when optimized for maximum performance, they yield speeds of approximately 10-20 TFlops on today's leading HPC systems.

Cross-anatomy domain adaptation is a highly demanding task due to the extensive variations in anatomical structures between domains. This research introduces Contrastive Semi-supervised learning for Cross-Anatomy Domain Adaptation (CS-CADA) to tackle this challenge. CS-CADA is a contrastive learning method that leverages both unsupervised in-domain and cross-domain data to achieve accurate segmentation results. By employing a contrastive loss function, CS-CADA enhances the separation of adapted codes between domains and reinforces the completion of missing annotation masks on the source domain. This is done through a multi-domain code representation, where a domain-invariant code is used for adapted codes and a source-domain-specific code is employed for mask completion. Moreover, CS-CADA introduces a contrastive retrieval loss to penetrate deeper anatomical structures. This is achieved by training a encoder-decoder network to synthesize source-code representations and recovering the real source-domain images through code-to-image decoding. This encourages the encoder to extract detailed code representations that can penetrate deeper into anatomical structures. Comprehensive experiments on two public datasets demonstrate that CS-CADA boasts highly accurate segmentation results and outperforms existing cross-domain adaptation methods.

We provide a revised analysis of a suggestion made by Chamseddine and Arnowitt in 1983. They proposed that supergravity's 4-dimensional theory could be consistently developed if the dimensionality is increased to 5, with specific boundary conditions imposed on the extra dimension. We offer an alternative explanation as to why this might be the case, drawing from the principles of quantum mechanics, specifically the concept of nilpotent symmetry, to demonstrate that a proper understanding of 3D+1 supergravity can only be achieved if the theory includes 5-dimensional configurations, and that this is necessarily coupled with a 4-dimensional 'boundary' layer, with the two components being distinct in their physical properties.

We've proposed a novel plasma waveplate concept that uses a specific type of plasma layer to compensate for magnetic field effects on X-mode microwaves in magnetized plasmas. Theoretical modeling revealed that a substantial impact can be achieved with a thin (approximately 1 cm) layer, albeit this thickness varies significantly with electron density and magnetic field strength. Laboratory experiments confirmed the waveplate's effectiveness, yielding a 10:1 ratio of X-mode to O-mode power transmission. This technology has the potential to significantly enhance the performance of magnetized plasma X-band transmission lines.

We investigate the significant contribution of the tau electric dipole moment, made exceptionally sensitive by the KOTO and FASER$\boldsymbol{2.0}$ experiments, to the two-Higgs doublet extension of the Standard Model. By analyzing the CP-violating interactions connected to the $\tau$ lepton, we establish a relationship between the tau electric dipole moment and the $\tau \to \eta \mu$ decay rate. Furthermore, we identify the parameter region that maximizes the tau electric dipole moment, with the condition that it remains below the 10$^{-24}$ e.cm threshold. With the added constraint of the $\tau \to \eta \mu$ decay rate being greater than 10$^{-17}$ times the Standard Model value, we determine the most plausible region of the two-Higgs doublet parameter space.

This paper examines rank metric codes with high error correction capabilities, either in the context of average or maximum error magnitudes. We provide guidelines for constructing good rank metric codes, either individually or as part of a family, ensuring that they can accurately correct errors of a specific magnitude. Specifically, we discuss the creation of high-density rank metric codes with minimum weight $\rho$ and the development of codes with specific large minimum weights. We also highlight potential applications and related research opportunities.

The structure of conserved current block expansions in two-dimensional conformal field theory is examined for both AdS$_2$ and AdS$_3$ geodesic operators, which have the same primary fields. Our analysis reveals a representation disparity between these two contexts, indicating a non-trivial cross-talk between them. Using the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator form, we derive an explicit formula for the two-point function of these conserved current blocks in CFT$_2$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator form can be related to the semi-classical string field $\beta$-function through the AdS/CFT correspondence.

We used the $35^{th}$ edition of the Dark Energy Survey (DES) data to evaluate the effectiveness of lensing reconstruction, specifically focusing on a comparison between traditional and neural network methods. For this analysis, we created multiple mock galaxy samples with associated lensing maps, and then applied various methods to these samples. Firstly, we found that deep learning approaches outperformed traditional estimators and offered a level of flexibility in lensing reconstruction. Secondly, we discovered that the choice of neural network architecture has a significant impact on its performance, and that a specific variant can yield comparable results to an optimal custom network. Lastly, we estimated the uncertainty associated with lensing field reconstruction and implemented a format compatible with current cosmological analyses. Using this information, we calculated the mass power spectrum and the mass-velocity power spectrum, and has made the code and results publicly available.

In 2000, D. Gelfand and S. MacPherson defined combinatorial differential manifolds, introducing a method for representing these objects as various subgraphs of a differential manifold. We build upon their work by establishing an equivalence between their definition and the concept of control graphs in the context of R. Ghosh's control grid framework. This equivalence enables the use of grid-theoretic properties to analyze combinatorial differential manifolds. Furthermore, we demonstrate that several key parameters related to these objects are actually apex parameters of the control graphs, which allows us to apply existing bounds to obtain new upper limits for the number of vertices in certain combinatorial differential manifolds. We also introduce the concept of layered control graphs to achieve higher vertex densities than previously possible and provide examples of highly dense combinatorial differential manifolds.

The type II supernova SN~2020jfo was particularly notable due to its unusually long duration of about three years of luminosity in excess of $10^{40}$ Watts and its distinctive double peak. By matching its light curves from various wavelengths, identifying essential elements such as hydrogen, iron, nickel, silicon, and hydrogen isotopes, we were able to interpret its prolonged radiation and double peak as a consequence of two explosive events. The first event, which occurred about 13 days after the supernova's initial outburst, was characterized by a massive nickel release that quickly produced a significant amount of energy through numerous gamma-ray interactions with supernova electrons. This nickel release also created numerous gamma rays in the process. The second event, which occurred about 110 days later, revealed an unusually high level of iron and nickel production with very little nickel release, which resulted in a much longer duration of luminosity in the form of iron lines after the second peak. With the help of a rationalized line identification, we were also able to determine an unusually high level of iron and nickel production in SN~2020jfo with levels about five times the solar average, which is unusual for a typical type II supernova. The unique characteristics of this supernova, along with its extended radiation, further cements its place as one of the most atypical supernovae ever observed.

A cross-like image, generated using a simple model, is analyzed to understand its components' alignment with a lobster-eye optics system. By interpreting the image's orientation, or azimuthal rotation angle, we can identify how it relates to specific parts of the system. It is determined that the angle is indicative of the optical path's location within the system's acceptance angle and its corresponding projection on the detector. Furthermore, based on the angle, we can determine if a particular part of the cross belongs to the system's inner or outer region. In addition, we demonstrate that the cross-like image can be utilized to measure the size of a lobster-eye optics system's aperture.

We employ level set methods in conjunction with technique adaptations from viscosity solution theory to analyze second-order fully nonlinear partial differential equations. The method enables us to leverage algorithms for capturing interface dynamics between solution regions to derive existence and uniqueness evidence for a broad class of such equations, including those defined by Bellman-type operators.

Using an extensive dataset of dark matter halos from the IllustrisTNG-100 simulation, we assess the performance of two types of models in predicting halo masses. The density-only model, which is based on the relation between a halo's density and the surrounding cosmological density, is particularly effective, particularly for low-density halos. When subjected to 13 distinct tests, this model achieves a high accuracy, with a difference of 0.06 times the standard deviation from the expected value. Combining density and velocity fields enhances the model's accuracy even further. We examine the level of agreement between different models and observations. In all cases, we find a very low discrepancy of less than 0.5, indicating that the models are highly accurate. We also explore the level of agreement between different models and each other's predictions. Interestingly, we find that the velocity-based model predicts a higher halo mass than the density-based model, with a discrepancy of 0.25 times the standard deviation. We analyze the level of agreement between models and the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations. When subjected to a high amplitude of perturbations, the density-based model performs better than the velocity-based model. However, when subjected to a low amplitude of perturbations, the velocity-based model performs better than the density-based model. We examine the level of agreement between models and the amplitude of initial vector perturbations. When subjected to a high amplitude of vector perturbations, the density-based model

We introduce a semi-supervised version of the Convolutional Neural Matrix Factorization (CNMF) method, adapted for piano transcription, and comprehensively evaluates its variants, the original CNMF method, and a range of top-performing low-rank factorization techniques alongside supervised deep learning methods on two datasets. Our research demonstrates that the semi-supervised CNMF approach surpasses CNMF and nearly matches its performance with only a small amount of labeled data, achieving a notable improvement of 2.5 points in Mean Note Error compared to the baseline.
