In Bayesian mixture modeling, imposing a Dirichlet process prior on densities typically results in non-identifiable admixture weights. We investigate the effect of a specific variation of this approach, placing a Dirichlet process prior on the base measure with respect to a structured parameter set, which corresponds to densities that share a common function form, particularly polynomial densities. We derive a condition for the uniqueness of admixture weights in this case and develop an efficient algorithm for their recovery, demonstrating improved performance compared to standard methods. We provide a theoretical guarantee of convergence for this algorithm and evaluate its effectiveness through simulated and real-world experiments.

A calculation of two-loop corrections to the anomalous dimensions of twist-four operators in N=4 SYM theory using the AdS/CFT correspondence has been performed. Anomalous dimensions for operators like W_n~4[U_n] were calculated at two loops in the AdS/CFT framework, confirming the predicted relationship with elliptic beta functions. This confirmation extends previous one-loop finding to two loops. Furthermore, the calculation of anomalous dimensions for other twist-four operators like W_n~4[S_n] and W_n~4[Γ_n] revealed specific two-loop corrections that match those proposed by Anastasiou and Büchner in 2008. This agreement provides further evidence for the AdS/CFT correspondence.

Approximately 15 years have passed since GPU computing has been integrated into various High-Performance Computing (HPC) systems, revolutionizing the field of scientific simulations through Accelerated Parallel Processing Units (APUs). As high-performance applications with extensive data sets face significant challenges in managing GPU memory efficiently, researchers like Chen et al. introduced DynaSOAr, a cutting-edge dynamic allocation framework for memory management on GPUs. By incorporating a hierarchical sorting approach with a load-balanced strategy, DynaSOAr significantly enhances performance and free memory recovery compared to traditional GPU memory allocators. Specifically, DynaSOAr exhibits improved performance in benchmark tests and, in industry practice, it demonstrates superior results in memory allocation tasks for real-world applications, ultimately leading to significant advancements in GPU memory occupancy. As a result, applications with extensive data sets can now efficiently utilize GPU memory, unlocking more computational power for APU-based HPC systems. With DynaSOAr's proven track record, its code has been open-sourced, and the framework is now widely available on GitHub at the specified URL.

This research paper investigates the boundedness and continuity of operators between generalized mixed Morrey spaces, particularly focusing on the Morrey operators and their applications. Firstly, the paper establishes the boundedness criteria for Morrey operators to act on $Q_{s,p}$ spaces, followed by exploring the continuity conditions for these operators in different operator spaces, including those with compactness properties. Moreover, the study provides a discussion on the approachability of these conditions through local mean estimates, a significant aspect in the analysis.

We investigate the effects of spin-orbit coupling and interactions with YSR states on single atomic magnets or pairs of magnets using the NewNon-Collinear Numeral Method. Our study examines the impact of varying YSR states on single atomic magnets or pairs of magnets located within different regions of the Fermi surface, particularly around the point (0,0.5$\pi$) where YSR states exhibit no significant influence. We find that for our model system, a pair of magnets exhibits more robust spin-orbit-induced peak position changes than a single atomic magnet. This distinction highlights the importance of considering multiple atomic magnets in theoretical analyses of spin-orbit-induced peak position changes.

Recently, Implicit Masking was introduced in FourierMask, enabling the creation of higher-resolution segmentation masks using implicit functions in a Fourier-based representation. However, training this model proved challenging due to its low-resolution initial condition, limited input channels, and the absence of direct connectivity between neural networks. To overcome these difficulties, we develop a novel Neumann boundary condition-based loss function that allows the model to generate higher-resolution segmentation masks. Moreover, we propose an efficient grid marching algorithm for evaluating the model's implicit function, which yields significant computational speedups. Ultimately, our approach achieves superior performance, surpassing the baseline model by 4.16% in terms of surface Dice score, and we make publicly available both the code and model pre-trained on the MindScope dataset.

We provide a novel proof that any minimal disk in Euclidean 3D space, of finite area, must be topologically equivalent to a standard disk. Additionally, we demonstrate that if a submanifold, of dimension d, is embedded in the Euclidean space R^n, with its boundary consisting of d components, and if the submanifold's distance to the closest parallel submanifold is greater than a specific value, then it must have a complete, bounded minimal disk similar to that found on the d-sphere in R^n.

The technique of cloud structure analysis through shape and size measurements in satellite images has a notable limitation: it only works for clouds with visible bases and surrounding veil clouds do not fit this criterion.  This limitation is addressed by introducing a new concept, "veiled core", which is the central part of a cloud that is opaque and hides the cloud's base, while the outer parts create a veil.  By identifying the veiled core, which is visible in the satellite image, it is possible to estimate the cloud's effective size.  This method was tested with real data, including cloud systems over West Africa and South Asia, by comparing model predictions with actual cloud observations from space, which showed a strong correlation.  The results indicate that using the veiled core approach can accurately estimate the cloud's size, which in turn can be linked to dust emission rates, ultimately providing a better understanding of the dust's impact on solar radiation.  This method also offers a solution to another problem of cloud analysis, by allowing the estimation of multiple clouds that merge to form a large cloud system, which was a significant challenge with previous methods.

To examine the complex interaction between two distinct layers in ions, we have generated comprehensive data using particle-in-cell simulations for a scenario involving a thin, low-density secondary layer surrounded by a much thicker, higher-density primary layer. The scenario, which includes a negatively chirped laser pulse and an increasingly intense counter-field, is thoroughly investigated to better understand the accelerated ion dynamics. Our findings reveal a notable increase in ion acceleration within the secondary layer as a result of an electrostatic field generated by the counter-field's interaction with the primary layer. Additionally, our results indicate a significant influence of the counter-field on ion motion, with the option to control the acceleration process through the intensity of this field. A key observation from our simulations is the presence of a specific emittance profile, which could be utilized to improve the quality of ion beams. Finally, we have identified conditions under which a significant increase in ion acceleration can occur within the secondary layer, which may have implications for various applications involving ion beams.

We discovered two new transiting mini-Neptunes around the G-type star KOI-423, which lie within the habitable zone. These planets, named KOI-423.01 and KOI-423.02, have radii of 4.53 times and 4.69 times Earth's radius respectively, and orbit their star every 21.81 and 84.86 days. By analyzing light curves from the Kepler space telescope, we found these planets by identifying objects that blocked a specific amount of light as their host star passed in front of them during transit events. By examining the star's oscillation frequencies, we determined the density of these planets, which revealed that KOI-423.01 has a density similar to gas giants, while KOI-423.02 has a higher density due to its more substantial rock composition. Notably, KOI-423.02's mass was determined through radial velocity measurements, which indicated a mass of 7.45 Earth masses, allowing us to classify it as a super-Earth rather than a mini-Neptune. Given its location in the habitable zone, KOI-423.02 is considered a promising candidate for hosting conditions suitable for life.

We utilized a combination of computational modeling and experimental analysis to examine the behavior of carbon and nitrogen within TiO2, particularly when they occupy interstitial positions as opposed to replacing oxygen atoms. Our theoretical predictions, made using supercell methods and first-principles calculations, were verified by experimental data from Positron Annihilation Spectroscopy (PAS) and Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry (SIMS). In their interstitial state, C and N atoms behave differently from their counterparts in substitutional sites. Additionally, our results indicate a significant difference in the stability of C and N in TiO2 when placed in the [110] interstitial position as opposed to the [001] position. This distinction was confirmed by PAS and SIMS. Our findings also suggest that PAS spectral shapes can provide information on the location of these defects, and that C and N in TiO2 are more stable in the nanoscale than previously thought.

We have used data from semi-elastic top quark decays at 13 TeV with an integrated luminosity of 35 inverse picobarns to set upper limits on flavor-changing neutral current decays of the top quark. These include limits on direct electroweak flavor conversion as well as on indirect conversions influenced by Higgs boson interactions. Specifically, we have derived 95% confidence level upper limits on branching ratios of around 0.006-0.439% for direct conversions and 0.007-0.668% for indirect conversions, with precision increasing with larger top quark momentum thresholds. These findings represent the most restrictive limits to date on flavor-changing neutral current decays of the top quark.

The X-ray Integral Field Unit (X-IFU) is an instrument on the Athena X-ray Observatory that will provide high spatial and temporal resolution spectra of X-ray sources, allowing it to capture the dynamics of the intra-cluster gas and study turbulence in these clusters. X-IFU's onboard Data Reduction System will refine its observations, which are expected to be observed for about 300,000 seconds per year, to produce final data that can be used for scientific analysis. These data products will be the output of a full data reduction process, involving various steps from detection to parameter estimation, assisted by physical models to account for any particular features and phenomena, as informed by physical theories and observations. We review the various components of the X-IFU Data Reduction System, which includes a detection module based on a Maximum Likelihood approach, a source extraction module based on the Extended Flexible Image Processing System, a Spectral Extraction module based on the Fermi Fermi Science Tools, a Time Series Analysis module based on the HEASOFT routine granular, and a Parameter Estimation module using physical models, as well as a Background Estimation module based on Background maps, and a Multi-Frequency Analysis module based on the Athena X-IFU Wavefront Reconstruction Algorithm.

We have provided new, general lower bounds for the number of colors needed to edge-color a graph G in such a way that no set of F edges within G are all the same color, where F is a given subgraph of G. These lower bounds make use of the maximum number of vertices in F, its edge connectivity, and the chromatic number of the complement of F. We have shown that if F is a triangle, then its edge coloring problem has a lower bound of at least $\frac{3- \epsilon}{2}$ times the number of colors needed to color the complete graph on the same vertices as F, where $\epsilon$ is an arbitrarily small positive number. This proves a long-debated conjecture of Kieronski. We have also considered various special cases of the general problem, including those where F is an odd cycle, a star, or a path. These investigations raise several interesting open questions.

The Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) is the largest molecular complex in the Galactic Center, and its density structure exhibits anisotropy. Researchers have studied the metal content in the CMZ and found a non-circular distribution pattern. A new analysis of 1.3 mm continuum data from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter array, combined with previous data, reveals that the anisotropic density structure in the CMZ changes with scale. At small scales (~1 pc), the anisotropy is consistent with the influence of a bar-shaped potential. At larger scales (~5 pc), the anisotropy becomes more pronounced and aligned with the minor axis. This change in anisotropy may be caused by the formation and destruction of dense cores in the CMZ. Researchers estimate the core formation timescale as about 20 million years and the core destruction timescale as about 10 million years. Additionally, the analysis shows that the non-circular metal distribution pattern in the CMZ is a result of the interplay between core formation and destruction.

Most face recognition techniques rely on the entire face and don't account for the distinctive characteristics of eyes. They typically use face detection methods that consider the whole face's structural composition. In contrast, our eye-dedicated detection system, known as EyeFirst, ignores face patterns and focuses solely on ocular features' uniqueness. By doing so, it offers several advantages over conventional methods. Firstly, it needs much less training data, resulting in more accurate models with fewer neural network parameters. Secondly, it facilitates end-to-end face recognition without extensive finetuning, producing results that are surprisingly good. We've thoroughly evaluated EyeFirst through both theoretical and practical assessments, comparing it to the state of the art in face recognition and detection. Our findings are consistent with the hypothesis that eye-focused detection yields better results, albeit with some exceptions. Additionally, EyesFirst has demonstrated exceptional performance on real-world scenarios, outperforming the current state of the art in various scenarios.

Our investigation into the precision of quantum error correction in single-qubit systems reveals that even minor deviations can significantly impact the accuracy of this process. We find that, compared to qubits, qutrits are more susceptible to losing precision due to certain types of errors, especially those affecting the diagonal components of their state. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that the optimal size of a single-qubit system is approximately 1.43, as this value achieves the minimum variance in phase estimation with the most efficient scale being roughly 1.19. We believe our findings have important implications for the optimal design of small-scale quantum circuits.

To accomplish various scientific objectives with an IRF-like experiment, such as simulating real photons in dark matter searches or producing suitable conditions for dark force experiments, positrons must be created with high polarization. Specifically, we need more than 30% polarization to effectively mimic real photons or produce suitable conditions for dark force experiments. We have succeeded in creating highly polarized positrons through the production of real and virtual photon pairs, achieving over 31% polarization at an energy of 10 GeV. This achievement was made possible by using the existing IRF magnetic field system and manipulating existing limits on the polarized structure function of the electron to extract cross-section equations, followed by realistic simulation of existing data to refine these equations. These findings demonstrate that the existing IRF system holds great potential for achieving its research goals.

In this paper, we explore the polynomial diameter concept in finite groups. Specifically, we demonstrate that groups with polynomial diameter are characterized by a specific property: they contain a substantial number of conjugacy classes with small diameter, along with numerous nilpotent subgroups of relatively small rank. This characterization reinforces the underlying idea behind the polynomial diameter concept. Additionally, we establish an upper limit for the diameter of groups that are both solvable and of fixed, low character complexity. This limit is expressed in terms of the group's size and its conjugacy class distribution. We also present an example to show that this limit is indeed necessary. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of polynomial diameter nitpickers and explore the properties and consequences of this new class of group elements.

The presented work proposes a temperature sensor, based on the thermal expansion properties of silicon, which utilizes a mechanical bridge made up of silicon stripes to detect changes in their resistance at different temperatures. The bridge is incorporated into an amplifier circuit that converts the thermal expansion-induced strain into a proportional voltage. The voltage output is directly proportional to temperature, with a proportionality constant determined through mathematical modeling and experimental measurement. The proposed sensor's accuracy was tested with an experimental setup, yielding an error of less than 0.1K for a precision of $\pm$0.1K, which can be achieved with a 16-bit ADC. The results demonstrate that the sensor's resolution and inaccuracy standards exceed typical specifications for thermistors and PT100 sensors.

The ideal magnetohydrostatic equilibrium equation is used to compute the interplay between toroidal and poloidal components of magnetic fields in stars. It is demonstrated that a specific equilibrium configuration, characterized by interconnecting toroidal field loops and a poloidal field generated through them, cannot be unstable according to the criterion of Rayleigh. The interconnecting poloidal field component helps in reducing the growth rate of any slightly disturbed state. The condition of mutual stability between the toroidal and poloidal components occurs when the magnetic pressure is distributed equally within these components. The ratio of toroidal to poloidal magnetic field strength is defined as the safety factor, and it must be less than one for the toroidal component's stability. The toroidal field's stability can be ensured through the rotation of the star, and the effect of this rotation on the stability depends on the angular rotation velocity's magnitude in relation to the universal angular rotation velocity. If the universal angular rotation velocity is greater than the star's rotational velocity, the toroidal field remains stable. On the other hand, if the star's rotational velocity is greater than the universal angular rotation velocity, the toroidal field becomes stable, and this effect intensifies with increasing rotation velocity. The rotation of the universal angular rotation velocity aids the stability of the toroidal field component, and this assistance increases with higher rotation velocities.

Our investigation proposes a novel perspective on the irreversibility inherent in renormalization group flows. By drawing a comparative analysis between the equations that govern RG transformations and those of fluid dynamics, we establish a analogous relationship between these two systems. In this comparative study, we establish that the RG equations can be viewed as a form of diffusion processes occurring within the space of coupling constants, with the added component of conservation of certain parameters. Our findings indicate that the irreversibility present in RG flows can be attributed to the inherent properties of diffusion processes, with the effect of obstacles in the potential influencing the direction of flow. Furthermore, we observe that the Onsager-Machlup theory, commonly used to quantify the irreversibility of fluid flows, can also be applied to describe the irreversibility of RG flows. With this new perspective, we are able to successfully model the complexity of RG flows using the concept of action and action angle variables, which enables us to identify distinct phases of the Wilson action. Additionally, our method allows us to determine the Lyapunov spectrum of the RG flows and the complexity of the trajectories within the phase space, which further reinforces our understanding of the irreversibility present in RG flows.

Audio search engines for music, such as searching for lyrics and audio, diverge from traditional web searches due to their unique challenges. A precise search engine would effectively navigate music databases, accurately match audio recordings, and efficiently locate desired lyrics. However, music search engines often rely on basic prefix matching techniques, neglecting more efficient methods. To address this, we introduce Rimo, a regex-based search engine designed to handle music data, leveraging lightweight indices and efficient navigation tools to accommodate complex queries and large music databases. Rimo's performance is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments, showcasing its capability to handle complex queries and extensive music databases with superior efficiency and accuracy. Furthermore, Rimo's source code is freely available for download, enabling further development and customization.

This work builds on a earlier concept introduced in arXiv/1712.06534, relating topological groupoid extensions to gerbes over topological stacks. We now generalize that idea to stacky groupoid extensions, which we connect to gerbes over Deligne-Mumford stacks through a similar generalized language. This generalized framework also allows us to view a topological groupoid as a stacky groupoid over a discrete stack. We also establish a relationship between the cohomology of a topological groupoid and its extension, which we then apply to a related problem within topological field theory.

Our research examines the mass evolution of molecular cores for a group of 34 objects, all of which have the potential to form stars of massive nature. These cores were first identified through the detection of submillimeter continuum sources and later tracked over time in both their molecular core and star-forming disk forms. Observations taken at an initial stage of 1.9 years and a follow-up after 11-13 years revealed a notable pattern where the mass of the molecular cores increased by an average of 0.03 solar masses per year, with a standard deviation of 0.03. However, when considering the extremely low-mass objects, a much higher variation of 0.17 was recorded. Furthermore, it was observed that the mass growth rate of these cores correlates strongly with their low-to-moderate mass range, implying that the mass accumulation process reaches its peak before the star formation process begins. Consequently, the mass growth pattern of these cores, specifically those with masses up to 200 solar masses, suggests a limited time frame for the star formation process to take place.

Our research demonstrates that finite Godel algebras are uniquely equivalent to finite forest-like structures known as prefix forests, which are a natural extension of regular forests. This comparison forms the basis for an innovative interpretation of classical logical operations like the negation, conjunction, and disjunction using the basic actions of adding, moving, and merging branches within a prefix forest. Additionally, our study reveals that the dual description of finite Godel algebras, presented in the context of lattice theory, mirror the structure of prefix forests. This concept allows us to visualize complex mathematical proofs involving Godel algebras and use the intuitive understanding of prefix forests to solve them. By extending our findings to include Boolean algebras, we demonstrate that our prefix forest model also accurately represents the operation of biconnected component merging, or fusion. Furthermore, we show that our method of defining the operations of the Godel algebras using the negation of elements can be reinterpreted as a form of the Kleene star, or repeated application, of the corresponding Boolean fusion operations.

In 3D LiDAR data classification, using contextual information from nearby points can significantly enhance classification accuracy. This technique is particularly beneficial for automating the annotation process of large-scale datasets. We propose an iterative, neighborhood-aware voting system to incorporate contextual information. This method involves generating multiple classification results for each data point from diverse contexts, followed by an iterative process to combine the results based on contextual insights. Our approach is particularly effective at distinguishing composite classes and reducing false positives/negatives. This method achieves a class-AUC of 0.926 in our benchmark dataset, outperforming existing methods using contextual information. Additionally, this method demonstrates scalability and practical application in real-world scenarios.

Classical operations of differentiation and integration preserve the status of a function as positive definite when applied to elements that maintain a specific symmetry pattern, known as zonal functions. This paper investigates the impact of applying quantum mechanical operators, specifically the Hamiltonian and Lagrangian, to zonal functions. We demonstrate that these operations result in a loss of positive definiteness and provide an alternative, modified approach that maintains positive definiteness. This alternative method is then demonstrated with specific examples, including the application to zonal functions of order two in Euclidean space.

The discovery of a possible connection between ultra-high-energy cosmic rays and neutrinos has been explored for an possible explanation of the scarcity of cosmic ray events exceeding the threshold of $5.0 \times 10^{20}$ J. Using extensive air shower observations from neutrino detectors and cosmic ray arrays at high-altitude sites around $5.8$ km above sea level in the Andes, the Pacific, and the Karakoram, this research examines the composition and direction of cosmic rays beyond the threshold of $5.8 \times 10^{19}$ J in a way that is independent of atmospheric ablation. It also provides a more precise estimate of the cosmic ray energy spectrum up to $5.8 \times 10^{20}$ J and a new approach to reducing systematic uncertainties in multiple detectors at the same location through an in-situ calibration method in neutrino detection.

Theoretical models predicting the flow of liquid foams under pressure have been largely confirmed by experiments, which indicate that the viscosity of these mixtures is proportional to the square of the pressure, depending on the foam's structure and a "roughness factor" that represents the irregularity of the surface between adjacent bubbles. Despite the importance of this factor in determining the foam's viscosity, the roughness factor itself has not been a subject of extensive study, likely because it is difficult to measure directly. In an attempt to address this gap, we propose using data from capillary rise experiments in addition to cell size measurements to gain a more accurate understanding of the roughness factor. By applying this new method to existing experiments under different pressures and temperatures, we aim to explore its application to different types of liquids and determine the factors that influence the roughness factor within the same bubble structure. Furthermore, we hypothesize that in addition to influencing the foam's viscosity, the roughness factor may also impact its ability to heal from injuries.

In our investigation, we sought to excel in the ACAS XIV obstacle avoidance task, using a dataset of simulated scenes photographed by a moving camera. We realized that conventional convolutional neural networks are highly effective, but struggled with a critical issue: they often confuse relevant, moving 3D objects with insignificant, stationary background, hindering their ability to navigate safely. To overcome this, we leveraged ensemble-based, state-of-the-art image recognition techniques to combine multiple convolutional neural networks, each trained on diverse, transformed versions of the input images. By doing so, we significantly improved the accuracy of our model in classifying critical, moving objects and reduced the confusion with insignificant, background objects, thereby enhancing its ability to navigate safely. Moreover, we demonstrated the benefits of using an ensemble-based approach through comparative experiments, showcasing its capacity to handle complex, real-world scenarios and highlighting its potential for preventing mid-air collisions.

The interaction between surface tension and rotating liquid in a Hele-Shaw cell is studied numerically to investigate the effects on various states and their stability. The calculation is performed for a scenario where the inner cylinder rotates at a non-uniform speed and is surrounded by a narrow gap filled with a liquid of varying viscosity and surface tension. The results show that reducing surface tension has several consequences: it increases the stability of the laminar state, expands the range of the Taylor-Poiseuille state, and decreases the location of the transition to the Taylor-Poiseuille state as the cylinder's rotation speed increases. Furthermore, surface tension is found to influence the stability of the spiral state depending on the liquid's viscosity. Additionally, the analysis reveals that the Assael-Liouville equation can be used to model this phenomenon when the surface tension is low.

We introduce an average work quantity, dissipated work, which decreases over time as it corresponds to the average internal microwork done by a microstate in a many-body system and confirm its decrease for an out-of-equilibrium Ising spin chain using two methods.

Our study provides the first comparison of the relative abundances of CCH and CN radicals derived from cyclopentadiene and benzene, conducted using a laser-ablation, flow-cell technique coupled with discharge-laser spectroscopy. The comparison reveals a higher (CCH)/(CN) ratio in cyclopentadiene ((CCH)/(CN) = 1.58 ± 0.30) than in benzene ((CCH)/(CN) = 0.46 ± 0.18), which can be attributed to the greater effectiveness of cyclopentadiene in delocalizing its electron density, thus more efficiently producing the more stable CCH form.

We introduce a novel attention mechanism called "look-ahead attention" that enables neural machine translation models to consider the future context and potentially improve performance. By incorporating this mechanism, we demonstrate the significant benefit it yields when combined with the widely adopted inverse transformation attention, leading to substantial advancements in translation accuracy. Furthermore, look-ahead attention proves highly effective in utilizing future context to a similar extent as inverse transformation attention, but with a key difference - it relies solely on the attention weights rather than the entire hidden state of the encoder. Consequently, look-ahead attention offers a compelling alternative to inverse transformation attention that facilitates easier integration of future context. We validate the performance of look-ahead attention through rigorous evaluation on three assessment sets of the WMT translation tasks.

The Grids and Clouds (G&C) research community has adopted a translational approach, closely collaborating with industrial partners to successfully develop and apply grid computing technologies. This approach has led to significant advancements and numerous practical implementations. Despite the wealth of knowledge generated within the community over the years, there is a noticeable lack of documentation and dissemination of results among the community members. This special issue aims to address this gap by featuring extensions of prominent G&C research projects, as well as inviting contributions from the community to fill this informational void. In the following sections, we provide an overview of the selected projects, a thematic analysis of the community's working approach, and a perspective on the future of G&C research and development.

We've developed a cosmological multifield model using semi-simple Lie algebras, 
which leads to a complex system of partial differential equations. These equations 
evolve the model's parameters, resulting in a variable universe universe with changing 
cosmological parameters. Notably, our calculations indicate that the model's viscosity 
coefficient correlates with the rate of dark energy development, which could be explained 
by the presence of viscous dark energy. Furthermore, our research shows that the model 
can be interpreted through the lens of string theory, specifically with the presence of 
gravitons and their interacting effects on cosmic expansion.

Research into curiosity focuses mainly on intrinsic curiosity, but a new study reverses this trend by examining how interest in others affects an individual's curiosity towards new information. Based on peer influence theories, a survey was conducted to gather data from over 200 participants, who expressed their own and a peer's opinions on various topics. The results showed that workers with higher levels of core self-evaluations are more influenced by their peers' curiosity, but this only applies when they believe their peers hold higher status. Additionally, it was found that when opinions are diverse, individuals are more curious if they think their peers are more curious, but this effect disappears when opinions are uniform. A theoretical framework was also proposed to explain these findings, and it was tested with additional data, yielding supportive results. Overall, the findings highlight the significance of peers in curiosity development and suggest that social curiosity can drive curiosity towards new information.

We introduce a Python library that allows us to leverage graph Matérn Gaussian processes, making it easier to use these processes in settings with mini-batch data and when the model's parameters aren't constrained naturally. This library provides an efficient way to train these processes on large datasets by utilizing sparse and vectorized implementations of the graph Matérn Gaussian process, and has been designed with convenience in mind to make it simple to integrate these processes with stochastic variational inference methods. We also include the graph Matérn Gaussian process as part of our library's implementation of exact and approximate Bayesian methods for time series, regression, and classification.

In monitoring and responding to changes in urban road networks, both traditional static sensors and mobile vehicles holding valuable information play crucial roles. This paper proposes a model where ridesourcing vehicles are utilized as mobile sensors that collect data and contribute to network awareness. The goal is to determine optimal locations for deploying traditional sensors, as well as optimal routes for the ridesourcing vehicles, with the aim of maximizing the coverage and reliability of sensing capabilities while adhering to time and battery constraints. This problem is framed as a Constrained Min-Sum problem and tackled through a meta-heuristic approach, yielding a higher-quality solution than existing methods. Furthermore, the paper investigates practical implications and realistic assumptions by leveraging real-world data from Ridehailing companies in China.

We've performed an evaluation of the $J/\psi \to \text{invisible}$ decay using LHCb data from proton-proton collisions at 7 and 8 TeV, with an integrated luminosity of 3.0 fb$^{-1}$. This decay has contributions from initial states with dark matter and its various interactions with nucleons. By accounting for these processes, we determine relevant limits on the cross section for dark matter-nucleon scattering. If we assume the dark matter has a mass greater than 100 GeV and a certain spin properties, we found the cross section constraint to be around $10^{-41}$ to $10^{-42}$ cm$^2$ at 90% confidence. This method's sensitivity can be enhanced by utilizing full detector simulations with specialized dark matter detection simulations.

We introduce a variable stepsize version of the spectral general linear method (SGLM) that is particularly effective for approximating ordinary differential equations (ODEs) on nonuniform grid points. By adapting the method to a dynamic grid, we derive a condition that guarantees the same order of convergence as the original SGLM, despite using an optimal but variable number of grid points. Our implementation is shown to be an efficient and robust alternative to the classic Runge-Kutta methods, especially for problems with smooth solutions and optimal approximation of Lagrange interpolants. Our theoretical convergence analysis is matched by computational benchmarks that demonstrate the variable stepsize SGLM's precision and computational efficiency.

We introduce a comprehensive Python tool for our recently proposed methods, MFSSA, by replicating the experiments from our previous papers. This software encompasses two primary components: Structured Signal Analysis (SSA) and Matrix Factorization with Smoothness Constraints (MFSC). The SSA module encompasses three variants of MFSSA algorithms, along with necessary utility functions, while the MFSC module includes plain matrix factorization methods. Furthermore, we outline the implementation details and usage guidelines for both modules, along with an evaluation of the algorithm performance on the constructed datasets in contrast to the previously reported results. The source code is publicly accessible on GitHub, along with an accompanying example dataset that includes replication packages for the experiments described in the author replies.

Recent deep learning models have shown potential in automatically scoring written content, including essays, by predicting a numerical score based on the text's linguistic features. Nonetheless, research has indicated that these models may exhibit flaws in their evaluations, such as being overly sensitive to details and struggling to adapt to new, unforeseen circumstances. In the context of essay scoring, such issues could lead to problematic results, as they may overemphasize minor aspects and produce inconsistent ratings. This research investigates methods for addressing these challenges by implanting a degree of noise or bias into automatic essay scoring models, then exploring techniques to recover their original performance. Our findings suggest that while neural networks can indeed develop unstable behaviors, incorporating regularization can help mitigate this effect to some extent. Additionally, we discovered that even when these models produce inconsistent ratings, their underlying ability to understand the connection between language and score remains intact. As a result, we propose that evaluating automatic essay scoring models should distinguish between their capacity to grasp the underlying relationship between language and score, and their consistency in producing ratings.

This study explores the long-term behavior of a random walk with independent, identically distributed components, focusing on the impact of a concentration inequality on its asymptotic characteristics. We establish conditions under which the walk's typical distance from the origin grows according to a polynomial function, depending on an additional parameter that can influence the asymptotic distribution of the walk. This result is derived using a recent advancement in the literature, and subsequently, we demonstrate the connection between the walk's concentration and its asymptotic behavior. Additionally, we investigate conditions under which the walk's distribution converges to a non-degenerate limit, and provide concrete examples illustrating the effects of varying components' smoothness on the walk's characteristics.

Researchers are using plasma sources for various applications such as material analysis, gas processing, and radiation therapy. To optimize these sources, it's essential to understand plasma parameters like electron temperature and density. A review is provided of techniques used to measure these parameters through the interaction of plasmas with other fields, such as laser, magnetic, and electric fields. Additional factors such as measurement locations within the plasma, particle beams, and chemical composition are also considered in optimizing plasma sources.

A mathematical model based on difference equations is presented to examine the dynamics of entomopathogenic nematodes within a population of target insects. Specific variations of the Kermack-McKendrick model are considered to investigate the effects of nematode infection on their own reproduction and the birth rate of the target insect population, while also accounting for the phenomenon of superinfection. A numerical analysis of model-driven outcomes is conducted to explore various scenarios, including instances where infection leads to a decrease in the birth rate of the target insect population, as well as cases where repeated infections have no significant impact on this rate. Additionally, model parameters are compared to experimental data to verify their validity, and multiple models are coaxed into displaying similar behavior through a process called coincidence. This analysis, though conducted with nematode-target insect interactions in mind, can be applied to broader contexts involving host-parasite infections.

Our proposed W-shaped network ultimately achieves a high accuracy of 0.935 in the Lorraine (LO) dataset and surpasses conventional methods in terms of efficiency, reducing the number of nuclei misidentifications by 0.125 and the processing time per image by 0.5 seconds. Despite achieving excellent results on the LO dataset, our approach meets with limited success on the 2019 MICCAI Nucleus challenge dataset. To enhance its performance, we suggest a few amendments. 

In our research, we utilize the U-Net architecture as a baseline. Building on this foundation, we modify the network by incorporating additional branching layers in the encoding and decoding blocks, thereby increasing the number of learning parameters and upsampled feature maps. This enhanced design, dubbed the W-shaped network, is then applied to the automatic detection of kidney tissue nuclei. 

To optimize the network, we divide a large dataset into multiple chunks and employ a cumulative training approach. During this process, we observe the occurrence of over-learning, which is addressed by introducing a threshold to limit the acceptance of new parameter updates. 

Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed W-shaped network outperforms the baseline U-Net network in terms of accuracy, efficiency, and a balanced compromise of both. 

Furthermore, we examine the effect of encoding and decoding block complexity on the network's performance and find that increasing the number of layers in both blocks leads to a significant improvement in accuracy at the cost of processing speed. 

Ultimately,

Let's consider a number field $k$ and its completion $K$ at a prime $L$, along with local fields $K_v$ for every prime $v$ of $L$. Additionally, let's define local fields $K_{v_1}\otimes_k k'$ for every prime $v_1$ of $K$ that lies over $v$. Now, given isomorphic irreducible admissible representations $\pi_{v_1}$ and $\pi'_{v_1}$ of the special orthogonal group $SO(2d_{v_1}, k'_{v_1})$ or the symplectic group $Sp(2d_{v_1}, k'_{v_1})$, along with twists $L(\frac{1}{2}\otimes\pi_{v_1}, \psi_{K_{v_1}})$ and $L(\frac{1}{2}\otimes\pi'_{v_1}, \psi_{K_{v_1}})$ with the same rank for every prime $v_1$ of $K$ that lies over $v$, along with isomorphic local gamma factors $\Gamma_{\psi_{K_v}}(\pi_v, \otimes_{v_1}\pi_{v_1}, s)\cong\Gamma_{\psi_{K_v}}(\pi'_v, \otimes_{v_1}\pi'_{v_1},

The paper investigates the Hamiltonian path index (HPI) of graphs, defined as the fewest number of hamiltonian paths required to cover all pairs of vertices. We delve into various classes of graphs, determining whether their HPI is finite and, if so, its minimum value. Specifically, we examine the HPI of bipartite graphs, cubic graphs, and graphs with minimum degree greater than 2.

Research suggests that COVID-19's Apoptotic Ring Formation (ARF) pattern of cell death might be a key factor in the disease's pathogenesis and progression. By studying ARF in human bronchial epithelial cells and using a lung organ chip model, our findings show that these cells undergo ARF when infected with SARS-CoV-2. Furthermore, we observe that the virus's main protease (M^pro) is responsible for initiating the ARF response. Additionally, we discover that anti-inflammatory drugs such as LPS and GLP-1 can alter the ARF response, shifting from pyroptosis to apoptosis. Given the accessibility and established safety of these drugs, they may be a viable option for COVID-19 treatment by mitigating ARF.

External information can be incorporated into reinforcement learning through the discovery of external variables, essentially speeding up the exploration process by the factor of the number of possible actions. We introduce an efficient method for discovering these variables by leveraging the structure of action graphs, a technique that is computationally light enough for large-scale state spaces. Our algorithm works by identifying the most isolated nodes in the action graph, which corresponds to the most influential variables in the context of reinforcement learning. We demonstrate the benefit of this approach through a range of experiments, including a study of several well-known games from the ATARI library, by comparing it against multiple baselines, including a random walk. Our findings confirm that our method yields the highest returns in a significantly reduced number of visits.

Our research introduces HELMHOLTZ, a comprehensive verification tool for Michelson programs, the primary programming language for Tezos. This tool, developed in cooperation with the Tezos team, facilitates an automated and thorough analysis of contract parameters, allowing for the detection of potential discrepancies, as well as a symbolic execution-based method for checking the correctness of Michelson programs against their explicit specifications. Furthermore, HELMHOLTZ offers a range of features that contribute to improved code security, including anti-pattern and code-size audits. We have successfully applied HELMHOLTZ to a diverse range of Tezos contracts, including popular ones, and have reported the results to the Tezos foundation. We have also made significant contributions to the improvement of Michelson, recommending several language enhancements to the Tezos foundation.

Traditional convolutional neural networks and fully connected neural networks can be reinterpreted as graph convolutional networks, providing a unified framework that encompasses these networks. Within this context, node embeddings derived from graph convolutional networks are considered representations of nodes' intrinsic characteristics, independent of the graph structure. Building upon this concept, a novel approach is introduced that extracts high-quality node embeddings by minimizing the discrepancy between two distribution sets. Specifically, this method aims to identify a set of node distributions that can be grouped into two categories based on a classification function. The proposed algorithm is then demonstrated through two classification experiments, utilizing both synthetic data and real-world datasets, to evaluate its effectiveness. Furthermore, the theoretical optimization limitations of this algorithm are analyzed, and a computational efficient alternative is provided to tackle complex datasets. Experimental results show that this approach outperforms currently available node embedding methods.

In a recent study, we explored the properties of rotating hairy black holes in the context of Chern-Simons gravity, and found their entropy to be lower than that of similar black holes in pure gravity. Additionally, we established a connection between the Chern-Simons gravity theory and General Relativity through a 2nd order phase transition. This finding implies that rotating hairy black holes in Chern-Simons gravity can be viewed as having higher symmetry, and their properties as being governed by the principles of standard Chern-Simons theory. We then utilized this relationship to demonstrate that rotating hairy black holes' entropy can be determined through the Chern-Simons theory, and that this calculation produces the same result as when using the grand canonical ensemble in General Relativity. Furthermore, we demonstrated that rotating hairy black holes' entropy can be determined through the Chern-Simons theory, and that this calculation produces the same result as when using the grand canonical ensemble in General Relativity. Additionally, we found that rotating hairy black holes' entropy can be expressed as the difference between the Chern-Simons theory's and the grand canonical ensemble's entropy calculations, for the canonical ensemble.

Determining the fusion rules for non-invertible symmetries in quantum field theories can be a challenging task. We introduce the concept of crossing symmetry in the context of non-invertible symmetries, and demonstrate that it is a crucial constraint in deriving the fusion rules. We apply this idea to the Ising field theory in 2D, where the symmetries are described by parafermion currents. By utilizing the operator product expansion and the fusion algebra, we formulate a procedure to obtain the fusion rules for a given symmetry sector. We further demonstrate that non-invertible symmetries can give rise to non-trivial contributions in the partition function of a field theory, an effect that cannot be captured by mean-field theories. We illustrate this phenomenon in the 2D Ising field theory using the worm algorithm. Our study paves the way for exploring non-invertible symmetries in quantum field theories through the intersection of multiple symmetry sectors.

Ultrasound elastography quantifies tissue stiffness by evaluating axial and lateral displacement components within soft tissues. Axial displacement estimation is generally considered more accurate than lateral displacement, as it is less susceptible to image resolution constraints. This is particularly true for ultrasound elastography, as it typically suffers from limited lateral resolution. To enhance lateral displacement estimation, a new approach called multi-scale canonical correlation analysis (MSCCA) has been developed. In MSCCA, corresponding elements from different A-mode ultrasound graphs are matched and compared at varying frequency widths to determine lateral displacement. This approach is displayed as an improvement over conventional methods, such as the weighted strain filter (WSF), through numerical simulations and real-world elastography experiments. Compared to conventional methods, MSCCA, and WSF, the accuracy of the three methods was evaluated and compared to the WSF-based method through elastography examinations on human subjects. The results showed that MSCCA and WSF yielded similar accuracy improvements of about 2.5 times and 3 times, respectively, over conventional methods in elastography examinations.

Logical pseudocodes, which incorporate conditions into pseudocode syntax, have an added layer of safety and accuracy, addressing a widespread issue in pseudocode-based methods - the misuse of ill-defined pseudocodes. We demonstrate that former techniques employing pseudocodes are, in fact, instances of this improvement, albeit in a implicit manner. Our proposed framework for creating these advanced pseudocodes includes specific rules and formatting guidelines, which have been successfully applied to improve two well-known methods relying on pseudocodes. The enhanced versions of these methods have shown superior performance in machine learning settings compared to their original counterparts.

The concept of Boolean rainbow Ramsey numbers (BRR) is explored in this study, where a specific pattern is identified in a Boolean lattice with two distinct color schemes. This pattern, however, does not exist with only one color scheme. By defining a Boolean lattice with 2^n elements as B = {0, 1}^n, this work determines the Boolean rainbow Ramsey number for a specific pattern and small Boolean lattices. It is demonstrated that the Boolean rainbow Ramsey number for an ascending chain of two elements in a Boolean lattice with two color schemes is 4, and this number increases to 5 when using only one color scheme. Additionally, the same pattern with three elements in a Boolean lattice results in a Boolean rainbow Ramsey number of 9 with two color schemes and 14 with only one color scheme.

We develop a groundbreaking one-pass algorithm for creating a coreset in the $k$-means clustering problem. Unlike prior methods which require multiple iterations through the data, our coreset construction technique is highly efficient and achieves the minimum number of core points via a single examination of the input dataset. Furthermore, our algorithm's coreset size is directly proportional to the square of the number of clusters, making it particularly effective for large-scale $k$-means applications. Additionally, we demonstrate that our algorithm's coreset size is essentially optimal when compared to other one-pass algorithms. To further complement our coreset construction algorithm, we also derive an upper limit for the variance of points located within the coreset, which is proportional to the square of the number of clusters and is optimal in relation to the coreset size.

Grid-based worlds present complex decision-making scenarios, especially in pursuit-evasion situations, which often require extensive computation for optimal strategies. By breaking down a grid world into higher-level states known as superstates, agents can simplify their decision process while maintaining an understanding of the underlying global dynamics. We introduce an innovative approach that utilizes summary information about state transitions and their probabilities to efficiently construct a set of relevant superstates. Furthermore, we develop an active learning framework that identifies the most valuable data to be collected to enhance the accuracy of these superstates, thereby informing the most beneficial exploration policies. Through comprehensive simulations, we demonstrate that our approach not only produces high-quality superstates but also outperforms existing methods in terms of computational efficiency and effective exploration, even in large-scale scenarios and multi-agent settings.

A an n-tuplo de números inteiros não é transitivo se não puder ser rearrangido para multiplicar os números de forma exponencial. Definimos a função phi(n) como contando os pares não transitivos de n-tuplos. Esta função é explorada em seus primos e potências de números. Além disso, determinamos os limites superiores de phi(n) para n sendo um número primo e um poder de número.

Recent advancements in unpaired image-to-image translation using cycleGAN have been impeded by the reliance on predefined source codes, resulting in limited flexibility and interpretability. To address this issue, we introduce a new cycleGAN design that incorporates adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) layers, enabling the separation of translation expertise from image representations. Our design involves introducing two new runner layers: a source code generator and a runner encoder, with the former producing codes that are fed into AdaIN layers to guide the translation, and the latter using these codes to generate new source codes. We further introduce a code generator discriminator and a pair of cycle consistency losses to enhance the generation of these codes. To facilitate the exchange of expertise between the two domains, we include two runnen layers in the cycleGAN architecture. As a result, our method successfully transfers the expertise of two domains to a third domain with minimal additional effort, resulting in a significant improvement over the baseline. Our design also provides a theoretical foundation for a more flexible and general cycleGAN framework that can easily exchange expertise between multiple domains simply by replacing the source codes. To validate our approach, we conducted extensive experiments on the multi-domain image translation task using the CelebA dataset.

We introduce a groundbreaking, seamless method to compute the score of a conversation based on the joint representation of multiple dialogue states. This novel multi-view score function simplifies the challenging task of modeling dialogue actions and user intentions from raw dialogue data. By incorporating a shared hidden state for the entire conversation, our method leverages all dialogue inputs simultaneously to model dialogue actions, user intentions, and the relationship between them. This allows us to bypass the difficult task of automatic dialogue segmentation and dialogue act labeling. As a result, our method enhances the learning of dialog representations during end-to-end dialogue state prediction tasks, particularly in long and complex conversations. We thoroughly evaluated our model across three diverse dialogue datasets and consistently observed improved performance compared to baseline models.

This paper investigates the impact of an external potential on the Yamabe soliton equation derived from the conformal $\eta$-Ricci-Yamabe soliton equation, where $\eta$ represents a constant scalar field. We demonstrate that the equation can be transformed into the standard Laplace equation when the potential vector field is conservative, which can be expressed as the gradient of a scalar function. We further establish the uniqueness of the solution to the simplified equation within a defined boundary condition.

Our calculations using the angular momentum projection method, similar to those in T. Fukuda et al. (Phys. Rev. Lett. 129, 032501), effectively demonstrate the impact of high-spin rotational states within deformed halos on atomic density distributions. By analyzing various density scenarios, including elliptical, spherical, and triangular shapes, our findings reveal that multi-configuration rotational states can distinguish between covalent and atomic structures, particularly in instances where traditional approaches fail to differentiate between these structures. Furthermore, our results indicate that high-spin rotational states can facilitate the formation of deformed halos by promoting configuration coherence, and that such coherence can influence the behavior of atomic densities within these halos.

This paper introduces BasicVSR++, a highly efficient video restoration model.
Building on the foundations of BasicVSR, we fine-tune several elements including
input frames, prediction layers, and optimization techniques to achieve a notable
improvement in both accuracy and computational performance.
Specifically, BasicVSR++ demonstrates a notable 12% increase in PSNR compared
to the original BasicVSR, amounting to a $1.5\times$ speedup in frame processing.
Our work is significant as it provides a comprehensive video restoration model
capable of being utilized on devices with limited computational power.
Such as mobile devices, capable of processing $384^2$ video frames within a
second, at a cost of less than $8$ on GPU.
We have made BasicVSR++ available for public use on Neural Tile Cloud, a
cloud-based neural network platform.

We investigated the parton distribution functions for W and Z bosons within the leading logarithic accuracy and identified universal correction terms, which hold across various scales and processes. These findings can inform the development of effective theory approaches, such as effective field theories, in a way that is independent of the details of the underlying theory, effective field theory, and can be used to derive relevant scale relations, potentially providing more precise determinations of underlying parameters, such as the pole top-quark mass, and helping to control the theoretical uncertainty in total cross-section calculations for high-energy processes, such as those at a future 100 TeV collider.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using a single dynamics model that excels in all tasks may not be ideal, as this can lead to over-reliance on the model's exploration benefits being offset by its limitations in task switching. This concept is illustrated through an example involving a robot that must master two different skills in open environments. By comparing the outcomes of two methods - one where the same model is learned on both tasks and another where distinct models are learned on each task - it is demonstrated that having different models can significantly enhance the robot's ability to transition between tasks. Furthermore, we introduce an efficient algorithm that takes advantage of a set of pre-trained dynamics models, allowing the primary model to be updated at a reduced computational cost. This method pays for fewer computations during the primary update by temporarily switching to one of the secondary models, thereby reducing the necessary computations during the update process.

This paper explores how boundary presence affects the infinite-time behavior of solutions to differential equations on noncompact, multi-dimensional manifolds. We establish a key finding, proving that solutions exhibiting long-term stability (in the sense of eventual boundedness) must necessarily converge to zero as time progresses, under the condition of a noncompact manifold having compact boundary components. Additionally, we demonstrate that this stable behavior is linked to the presence of compact boundary components through a specific determinant expression, involving a novel integral operator. This discovery enables us to create a practical test for determining whether solutions exhibit stable behavior on a given noncompact manifold. Furthermore, we extend our stable behavior criterion to a broader class of equations and establish a relevant relaxation concept.

In 1936, Godel's first incompleteness theorem demonstrated that any sufficiently rich formal theory must lack completeness, unable to prove all true statements within its scope.  Two years later, Kleene transformed Godel's findings by establishing a fundamentally distinct, yet equally pivotal incompleteness principle.  Although largely overlooked, this secondary principle holds immense significance, as it reveals an fundamental limitation on the ability of any formal system to encompass all valid logical statements about theorems within that system.  In his 1938 book, Rosser built upon Godel's initial research and, in doing so, gave this particular incompleteness principle a name and a enhanced mathematical formulation.  Throughout this paper, we delve into a comprehensive examination of Rosser's work, including his contributions to the development and various applications of this particular incompleteness principle.  Additionally, we introduce novel systems to illustrate specific aspects of his findings.  In particular, we explore the concept of "diagonalization procedures" that underlie this incompleteness principle, and demonstrate its fundamental connection to the self-referential nature of logical statements within formal systems.

Hadamard's three circles theorem can be expanded to apply to monogenic functions in higher-dimensional space, specifically in n-dimensional space for n equal to or greater than three. This extension is confirmed through a related theorem that can also be applied to these dimensions. Furthermore, both theorems can be used together to prove a significant consequence: if a monogenic function f is bounded on three distinct circles within n-dimensional space, then it can be expressed as a product of two functions, one of which depends only on the radial distance from each circle.

A balanced subset of a large population can be rigorously defined as a random sample where the differences between the corresponding variables of the sample points are as small as possible. Unfortunately, due to the complexity of the problem, it is difficult to obtain a balanced sample through methods that rely on probability theory. In order to address this issue, a new algorithm called the Local Interchange (LI) has been developed, which allows for the efficient selection of a balanced sample. The LI algorithm originates from the Kalman filter and utilizes local minimization techniques. It has been proven that this algorithm reaches a balanced state in a limited number of iterations and the length of this path is directly proportional to the size of the sample. The LI algorithm can be applied to a broad range of selection scenarios and even works with variables that change over time. Furthermore, the algorithm has been implemented on a large scale using a cloud computing platform. The results show that the LI algorithm produces a balanced sample quickly, and the length of this path is directly proportional to the size of the sample. The LI algorithm can be used for not only selection methods but also optimization techniques and even works with variables that change over time.

We've been utilizing indirect methods such as stereo and monocular reconstruction
to constrain camera calibration, but our research suggests that direct regression
can yield comparable results with minimal required image information. Our study
involved conducting a large-scale evaluation of direct and indirect methods on
eight popular datasets, and our results indicate that our proposed direct
regression approach achieves similar accuracy to complex indirect methods with
fewer necessary image constraints. Additionally, our method demonstrates
robustness in cross-dataset evaluations. We've observed that direct regression
outperforms complex indirect methods in some cases and provides more accurate
predictions of camera parameters.

This work develops a variant of the conditional Wasserstein GAN, which we call the
regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, to enhance the generation of imaging data
posterior samples. The modification involves adding a deformation term to the
conditional Wasserstein distance, resulting in an interpretable objective function
that can be optimized via adversarial training. We demonstrate the effectiveness of
this approach in two applications: x-ray computed tomography and magnetic resonance
imaging. Our method can be employed in both single-image and multi-image settings.
We utilize publicly available reconstruction software to evaluate our method's performance.
We show that our approach outperforms conventional transference methods as well as
deep learning-based approaches in both applications.

This paper explores the concept of invariance in linear systems with fractional derivatives and integrals. We establish precise criteria for the condition of invariance to be satisfied, demonstrating that the relationship between invariance and stability is not necessarily direct. Additionally, we identify potential pitfalls in the literature due to the misuse of incorrect formulas for the derivative of a subspace. Our approach simplifies the approach of T. Tsuda, while building on the work of S. S. Daqaq and H. K. Khalil. Finally, we demonstrate the practical applications of our findings through specific examples.

Our investigation into the efficiency of multi-hop THz links utilizes a hybrid beam training method. At the THz link, we employ an iterative method that converges to an optimal precipitation cell weighting factor, which significantly improves data transfer speed from 0.51 bits/Hz to 0.79 bits/Hz. When combining this with dynamic beam training at both the THz and mmWave links, we integrate it into an overall backhaul reconfiguration framework, which maximizes the overall data transfer speed for varying THz link conditions, achieving a 50% reduction in delay compared to traditional methods, with an average delay of 0.23 seconds, and varying THz link conditions, achieving a 30% increase in average data transfer speed, with an average of 0.79 bits/Hz.

We've carried out radio and optical observations of the PSR B1133+16 system, covering 3000 hours over nearly 30 years.  Our data reveal 24 individual scattering screens between Earth and the pulsar, with 11 of these screens appearing as clear pathways for optical pulses to reach Earth.  While 9 of these screens fall within a relatively close range of 4.5 parsecs, a significantly larger distance of 13.7 parsecs is estimated for the screen that led to the pulsar's initial optical detection.  We also observed the time it takes for optical pulses to travel through the screens, known as the dispersion measure, to be significantly greater than the corresponding value for pulsar radio signals.  This discrepancy increases with the distance of the screens from Earth, with a value of about 0.5 times the standard expected rate for the closest screens and decreasing to a quarter of that rate for the screens furthest from Earth.  We note a significant increase in the beaming energy of optical pulses as they pass through the closest screens, with a maximum effect observed for the screen at a distance of 4.5 parsecs, with a value of about 8 times the standard expected rate.  We also note that the screens must be optically thin, with a width typically ranging from a few astronomical units to hundreds of astronomical units, with some variation depending on their distance from Earth.
