Deep learning models that use convolutional neural networks (CNN) have achieved remarkable performance in speech synthesis tasks. These models leverage periodicity in speech spectra, often using a simple two-module configuration. This method works well for speech, but a more complex Donkey-Klang game dataset might require a more sophisticated approach. By building upon existing periodical components with additional modules, our proposed cascaded network structure reuses existing periodical information while exploring broader spectral regions. This leads to the discovery of additional quasi-periodical patterns and significant improvements in model performance, particularly when synthesizing voices.

Human annotators expend considerable time and resources to manually label and prepare data for machine learning, a process that could be of greater efficiency with the aid of automated tools. Despite this, few developers integrate human instructions with data enrichment objectives, limiting the benefit of collaborative human and machine learning. To address this, we design a novel framework called  2DCED that transforms instructions represented in a graph-based structural format into a standard text-based format suitable for neural networks to operate on. This enables the use of standard text-to-text transfer learning models to generate data enhancements aligned with the original annotations. Our approach demonstrates enhanced performance when compared to data enhancement approaches that rely solely on machine learning, and is particularly effective with more complex annotations. The design also allows for the incorporation of quality control measures to ensure produced data is of adequate quality for use in machine learning training.

The current data sets from missions like Kepler and TESS, combined with the growing list of exoplanet characterizations from RV surveys, are driving the development of increasingly sophisticated atmospheric modeling tools. These models allow scientists to make informed predictions about the chemical composition of planets located within the habitable zones of various stars. Given the diversity of possible conditions, it is essential to create models that can accommodate different levels of sophistication, such as complex atmospheric reconstructions, post-processing analyses of spectral signatures, and consistent physical connections between planetary properties. In this work, a set of sophisticated models is used to investigate how the metallicity of a planet's host star, atmospheric depth, temperature, and pressure influence the formation of various gases, including CO, CO2, NH3, H2O, CH4, and N2. The models produce distinct output spectra for each combination of model parameters and star type, showing significant variability. Notably, the models tend to overestimate the abundance of gases like CO, CO2, and NH3 when comparing results for G and K-type stars, while the models tend to overestimate the abundance of gases like H2O, CH4, and N2 when comparing results for M-type stars. These findings have implications for the interpretation of future observational data and highlight the importance of accurate atmospheric pressure and temperature measurements in order to correctly interpret the abundance of various gases.

We've examined the impact of non-Majorana behavior at the end of qubits on the conformal field theory model, particularly the conformal fisherman's equation model, at finite temperatures using the 2NDSE approach. We found that a zero-energy peak, resulting from non-Majorana influences, follows a power-law pattern in relation to the Chern number, whereas it diminishes with increasing temperature. Additionally, we identified that the 1/N peak contribution, derived from the 1/N expansion, aligns with the power-law relationship when normalized by the interaction strength, and that this contribution, influenced by the Chern number, is determined by a universal constant in the large N limit, particularly 4.36 in the conformal fisherman's equation model, although this value may change with other models. We also established that the 1/N expansion of the conductance at finite temperatures includes a zero-bias peak contribution, characterized by a peak with a width proportional to the interaction strength, and that this peak widens with increasing temperature, ultimately merging into a curve as the temperature exceeds the interaction strength, a phenomenon that becomes more pronounced at larger N values.

We have designed a versatile platform called RoadAtlas to accelerate road maintenance inspections and facilitate the collection of up-to-date data on road conditions. Built in accordance with modern web development standards, RoadAtlas offers a user-friendly interface and seamless navigation for users to create and manage digital maps, configure survey projects, and collect spatial data. Furthermore, RoadAtlas integrates with existing infrastructure, leveraging GIS technology to animate traffic data, determine optimal survey routes, and process attribute data. We have also incorporated data validation techniques to ensure the quality and accuracy of the collected information. Additionally, RoadAtlas features data visualization tools, enabling users to review and assess the data they have collected. We have also developed methods for validating the quality of the collected data, including techniques for detecting inaccurate or anomalous readings.

For the unit bicategory of a finite wedge of spheres, we establish a correspondence between the topological Hochschild homology of a multiplicative sequence and the shadows formed by combining the spheres that make up this wedge. Using this connection, we demonstrate that the topological Hochschild homology can be expressed as a sum of shadows, with coefficients determined by the algebraic structure of the sequence. Furthermore, this decomposition yields an equation relating the Hochschild-Kostant-Serre theorem to the formula for the Euler characteristic of a finite wedge of spheres.

We introduce VGG-SS, a comprehensive sound source separation dataset consisting of 80 categories of monophonic sources. VGG-SS is crafted from a diverse collection of music streams on YouTube, comprising over 1000 hours of audio, and is designed to evaluate the complex sound source separation process. Unlike existing datasets, such as MUSDB18 and TUT-ACOSTA, which primarily consist of a limited number of classes and categories, VGG-SS presents a more intricate challenge for sound source separation models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of a state-of-the-art model, Conv-Tau-LowD, by applying it to both the large-scale VGG-SS dataset and the simplified version of it, and compare its performance to other methods, including ours, on the dataset. The code and data can be accessed through this link: https://github.com/ghoury/VGG-SS.

Deep learning models in Euclidean space have seen significant advancements, 
while graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as prominent paradigms in curved spaces, particularly in Klein space. Most existing GNNs are limited by their assumption of constant curvature and fail to capture the inherent non-constant curvature present in real-world networks. Furthermore, they often overlook the intrinsic geometric structure of networks. In an attempt to address these shortcomings, several researchers have proposed a new framework for graph representation learning based on Lorentzian geometry. This paper delves deeper into understanding the Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN), a type of GNN that utilizes the Einstein trick, in an attempt to improve the node feature representation learned through its embeddings. In order to analyze LGCN, this paper introduces a novel approach that translates the Einstein trick trick into a form compatible with constant curvature, allowing for the interpretation of LGCN as a type of hyperbolic graph convolutional network (HGCN). Through this, we demonstrate that HGCN yields more accurate node feature representations than existing methods. Additionally, we provide a theoretical framework that demonstrates the relationship between LGCN and HGCN, thereby shedding light on the parameters of LGCN. In order to validate our findings, this paper conducts an in-depth comparative analysis of LGCN and HGCN across a diverse range of networks with varying geometric structures.

We have provided stability results for an inverse problem involving a non-acoustic PDE. These results are based on an internal observation model that is numerically well-defined. Specifically, we have a nonlinear PDE of the Stefanis type, propagating wave equation, or a linear PDE of the Schr\"{o}dinger type. Our control and observation systems are located inside a domain $\Omega$. If we assume that the initial displacement and velocity for the Stefanis type equation, or the coefficient of non-homogeneity for the Schr\"{o}dinger type equation, or the coefficient $c$ for the wave equation are known, we can determine a unique solution. This is under the condition of sufficiently small data, without any regularity requirement. If we only know the initial velocity for the Stefanis type equation, or the coefficient of non-homogeneity for the Schr\"{o}dinger type equation, or the coefficient $c$ for the wave equation, a stability inequality is sufficient. This inequality is based on an internal observation model and a singular control problem. The same is true for the wave equation with a non-homogeneous density under the condition of sufficiently small data, without any regularity requirement. If we only know the initial velocity, a stability inequality is sufficient.

We introduce the concept of the Time-Space-Spin (TSS) effect in a combined optomechanical system consisting of an optical cavity connected to a spin system. Here, time refers to the temporal variation of fields within the cavity, space alludes to the geographic location of the cavity and its mechanical connection, and spin represents the intrinsic properties of the spinning electrons. A simple model featuring a single photon, a single spinning electron, and a mechanical component with a single degree of freedom permits us to illustrate this phenomenon. It is demonstrated through both theoretical modeling and simulation that the TSS effect arises due to the interaction between these three components, giving rise to unique effects such as the creation of antineutrino-like photons, spinning photons that exhibit separate temporal and spatial variations, and mechanical neutrino-like behavior induced by spinning electrons. Furthermore, neutrino-like photons and mechanical neutrino-like behavior can be directly observed with current technology.

We investigate the presence of atoms in u-calculus, specifically its presence within the semantics of knowledge and belief at a glance, and demonstrate that the resulting system possesses an infinite number of models and countermodels in conjunction with a small set of axioms. Furthermore, we establish that the addition of quantifier rules significantly enhances both the theoretical and practical tractability of u-calculus, and prove that certain combinations of rules yield both decidability and the ability to verify validity in a finite amount of time.

The Tsallis distribution has various applications in physics, mathematics, and sociology, and is closely related to the concept of entropy. However, its primary advantage lies in its basis for developing a generalized theory of conservative systems and the emergence of power laws. This concept is particularly useful in social systems, characterized by non-linear interactions and fragmented scaling, such as in urban development, organizational structure within companies, and political organization within nations. Using the example of presidential elections in the United States, this study demonstrates the Tsallis distribution's applicability and also explores its limitations, revealing that it can only accurately model data over a specific range, typically where the parameter k exceeds 5, and indicating that a more tailored approach is necessary to effectively apply the Tsallis distribution to complex social systems.

We've re-examined the perturbations of gravitational forces, incorporating mass terms, and our calculations indicate that these terms free up additional flexible modes in the theory, amounting to two degrees of freedom with positive energy, in contrast to the massless case which only offers one such mode. Additionally, our analysis confirms the creation of massless scalar particle, often referred to as graviton, and further reveals that the mass term allows for the separation of long-wavelength fluctuations from the Gravitational field, amounting to $M_{pl}^2 \phi \sim h_{00}/2$.

Verified is the proposed conjecture that planar completeness of extended double covers of signed graphs is proven, with a corresponding decision algorithm for this class of signed graphs. This is achieved by demonstrating that the problem of determining if an extended double cover of a signed graph has a planar representation is equivalent to a more manageable problem that can be solved using a known algorithm.

We have established previous theorems on Hamiltonian dynamics within quantum equilibrium states, specifically within categories of (i) complete integrability, (ii) chaotic dynamics governed by strange invariant measures, (iii) chaotic dynamics characterized by strange attractors, and (iv) equilibrium states that relatively persist. To build upon these findings, we have developed an analytical proof that these four categories of Hamiltonian dynamics are distinct from one another.

We offer a basic conceptual demonstration of negative temperature within a two-level system, utilizing visual representations of thermal equilibrium, by applying the Boltzmann distribution directly to these levels. A straightforward method for calculating a negative temperature is also demonstrated, and both approaches are mathematically equivalent. Further, we provide insight into these concepts through animations, available as supplementary video files.

We investigate the size of a restricted signed sumset, defined as the collection of integers that can be obtained by adding a fixed integer to each element of a given finite set of integers, with a focus on understanding how the structure of this finite set influences the size of the restricted signed sumset. By establishing upper and lower bounds in various scenarios, our findings provide insights into the distribution and organization of elements within the restricted signed sumset, revealing important implications for its size and coverage. Additionally, our research identifies key conditions under which the restricted signed sumset achieves its maximum size, as demonstrated by several illustrative examples. Furthermore, we present a bound that, while not definitive, serves as a crucial step in proving a more comprehensive bound, as well as examining the efficacy of different summing techniques in maximizing the size of the restricted signed sumset.

A key challenge in controlling colorectal cancer morbidity lies in adequately identifying and classifying colorectal adenomas. This process is mainly impeded by the extensive and random nature of screening colonoscopies, which leads to a massive task for medical specialists to examine and report on adenomas. To solve this problem, we propose a fully automatic system that uses deep learning techniques to enhance the efficiency of adenoma detection, classification, and grading. This system consists of a detection network, which uses a region proposal network to locate adenomas within the virtual chromoendoscopy images, and achieves an AUC-ROC score of 0.8481 in our dataset. The classification and grading system, which operates on the entire frame, utilize a multi-resolution residual network and achieve accurate results with an accuracy score of 0.8491, a macro F1 score of 0.8051, and a mean IoU score of 0.7551 in our dataset. This system's effectiveness was further verified by means of retrospective and prospective studies, which showed a high correlation between its predictions and specialist examinations, with an agreement coefficient of 0.7481 and 0.7325 respectively.

To tackle the difficulties posed by high-frequency scenarios in acoustic scattering, specifically the instability of gradient methods, we introduce an optimization approach that incorporates a non-Newton strategy on a customized manifold. The key innovation lies in the explicit inclusion of the absolute value operator within the operator equation, thereby transforming it into a more manageable form that respects the Newton-Krylov method's efficiency. The resulting algorithm, built upon the CKW reformation, is then applied to a model problem to demonstrate its performance. Furthermore, we derive a theoretical guarantee for the proposed method's convergence.

Water contents within recent Antarctic finds of the Benenitra (2.1 ppm) and Chelyabinsk (0.3-0.7 ppm) ordinary chondrite falls exhibit varying levels, with water content ranging from 0.3-2.1 ppm. When comparing this to the water content within Antarctic finds and typical falls, we discover a mean water content within Antarctic finds at 1.0 ppm, with a 1 sigma range of 0.5 ppm. Furthermore, we distinguish between water-rich (water content greater than 1.0 ppm) and water-poor (water content less than 1.0 ppm) Antarctic finds, with distinct populations in water isotope composition, mineralogy, and point defects within olivines. We propose a model in which water-rich and water-poor Antarctic finds originate from different collisional events of small bodies.

We've developed expressions for the scalar products and form factors of higher-spin XXZ chains, using the algebraic Bethe ansatz, and these results hold for both solvable and non-solvable sectors. Our derived formulae demonstrate the interconnection between these quantities and the monodromy matrix's eigenvalues, ensuring that our results for scalar products and form factors are transparent and straightforward to use. As such, our work offers a clear, in-depth examination of the XXZ chain's properties. Additionally, our results for scalar products and form factors can be applied to other, related models, such as the XXZ chain with diagonal boundary interactions, and have the benefit of being non-summed, thereby offering more comprehensive, unified understanding of these quantities.

This study tackles the challenge of zero-shot speech translation, specifically focusing on improving performance in few-shot settings. To achieve this, we introduce two novel architectures: a speech-agnostic encoder and a simultaneous multi-form encoder. The speech-agnostic encoder leverages pre-trained models to bypass speech encoding, while the simultaneous multi-form encoder uses a shared encoder for multiple forms of input, eliminating the need for speech-specific architectures. To further enhance performance, we incorporate a variety of forms (e.g., transcriptions, translations) through a multi-form encoder. Support for low-resource languages is addressed through the use of pseudo pairs to minimize reliance on real data in few-shot settings. Our experiments demonstrate significant gains, with average BLEU score increases of up to 7 points compared to baseline models. Results show that our proposed methods achieve top-performing scores in both zero-shot and few-shot settings, outperforming strong baselines by 5-11 and 8-14 BLEU score points respectively.

Long-range multipoles are crucial for accurately describing how systems of charged particles scatter electromagnetic radiation.  While dipole scattering is well-understood, higher-order multipoles, specifically quadrupoles and higher-order types, are more complex to calculate but are, in fact, equally essential for a comprehensive comprehension of light-matter interactions.  Although previous studies have focused on deriving explicit formulas for calculating these complex multipoles, there is still a lack of understanding regarding their fundamental importance.  In this work, an intuitive analysis is performed to demonstrate the challenging nature of calculating these multipoles through classical means and to showcase the advantages offered by a quantum chemistry approach.  Furthermore, the paper highlights the value of using a multipoles-based approach to optimize the scattering of light, as seen in the case of f-shells.

Using the Langlands program, we establish a connection between certain classical objects in representation theory and their counterparts in the context of Runge's work. Specifically, we show that under an appropriate transformation, Schur elements correspond to shifted Schur polynomials, and nilpotent orbits correspond to Higgs bundles in the context of algebraic geometry. These correspondences hold in the limit of large rank and are consistent with each other, forming part of a broader Harish-Chandra isomorphism. We demonstrate that the Schur element, which represents the multiplicity of a given representation in the symmetric algebra of the adjoint representation, is analogous to computing the dimension of a specific cohomology space, which is represented by the shifted Schur polynomial. Furthermore, we explain that the extreme values of the Schur element, which correspond to nilpotent orbits, have a counterpart in the geometric context, where they represent the endpoint of a ray in a cone of representation stability, and this cone is the same as that which gives rise to the shifted Schur polynomials through the Harish-Chandra isomorphism. This correspondence also holds for blocks of representations and their geometric counterparts, and it reveals a connection between the endomorphism algebras of simple objects in the category O and the geometry of nilpotent orbits or Higgs bundles, which are shifted by Demazure-Lusztig. We've developed a straightforward, multi-deskartment approach that maintains the consistency of dark parity symmetry, even in the presence of vacuum instability. Introducing a minimal, dark-electromagnetic field that connects the dark sectors, we've observed that this connection has a significant impact on both the stability of the vacuum and the dark parity symmetry. However, it also facilitates neutral Higgs boson mediated dark matter interactions, which can be constrained by dark parity symmetry. Furthermore, we've found that this approach can result in dark matter models that resemble the inert doublet model, but with the added benefit of vacuum stability and consistent dark parity symmetry.

We have developed a semi-phenomenological model to account for strong interactions and spin-orbit coupling in 3d and 4d transition metal oxides, incorporating the physics of these materials at multiple scales. This approach, which we call the Interacting Spin-Orbit Model (ISOM), successfully maps the extreme limits of these systems - from the weakly coupled itinerant picture to the strongly correlated, locally confined scenario - while also capturing the intermediate regime. Using ISOM, we investigate a variety of materials, including 3d vanadium dioxide and 4d strontium iridate, to gain a deeper understanding of how spin-orbit coupling, crystal field splitting, and interaction effects influence the materials' electronic behavior. In these studies, we identify the emergence of strong spin-orbit coupling, forced by geometric constraints in 4d systems, as a crucial factor in the formation of robust, isolated Majorana zeros in their Fermi surfaces. These findings demonstrate the utility of ISOM as a powerful analytical tool for a systematic, material-by-material examination of topological electronics in transition metal oxides.

We derive a relationship for relative I-functions of toric complete intersections with smooth components, establishing a connection in a modified version of the I-function format. Furthermore, we establish a simplified relationship for a specific subcategory of these complete intersections, resulting in a consistent framework that aligns with Kimura-Saito-Yokoyama's relationship in a more limited context.

We've been using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to analyze medical images and generate new images, but so far, most applications have focused solely on producing high-quality images. However, GANs have an unexplored potential in learning latent codes that could inform healthcare professionals about disease characteristics, treatment responses, and genotypic and phenotypic differences. Unfortunately, a significant challenge arises during the process of interpreting the learned latent codes due to the complex, high-dimensional nature of these codes. To overcome this limitation, we propose a method called Mutual Information-based Latent Space Learning (MILLS) to isolate the codes related to specific variables of interest, such as disease types or patient outcomes, by maximizing the mutual information between the latent codes and these variables. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we used MRI data from two different sources and showed that the learned codes can distinguish between diseases, predict outcomes, and even identify variables that healthcare professionals might be unaware of. Furthermore, our results indicate that our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques for variable-based latent space learning. The code for our proposed method is openly available on a public repository, along with detailed usage guidelines.

The complex nature of high-dimensional data makes it difficult to present in a clear and intuitive manner.  This challenge is addressed by ViDaExpert, a user-friendly software that allows for the interactive visualization of up to four-dimensional data sets using various techniques.  These visualization methods include bicolor mapping, heat mapping, tree mapping, scatter plotting, surface plotting, and network plotting.  ViDaExpert provides a simple and accessible interface for importing, exporting, and organizing data, as well as a range of customization options for the visualizations.  This software is particularly suited for use in small to medium-sized research groups, offering a set of features that make it especially useful for visualizing large numbers of small to medium-sized data sets.

This study explores the implications of using a higher-order two-dimensional monomial approximation on the approximation of a function over a single finite element, similar to recent findings regarding its impact on polynomial interpolation. We derive an key inequality involving the monomial approximation error, which enables us to establish upper bounds for the error resulting from the monomial approximation, Lagrange interpolation, and Bernstein--Bézier representation. These bounds facilitate our analysis of the accuracy of these representations, demonstrating how a smaller error can be achieved by increasing the order of the representation but, due to the nature of the error expansion, only to a limited extent. We also examine the condition under which the monomial approximation and Lagrange interpolation errors dominate respectively, which is crucial for ensuring that the monomial approximation or Lagrange interpolation most accurately represents a function over a given mesh element.
